speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago to-day, it was my sad duty to remind hon. members of this house of the first loss which death had occasioned in its membership in this new parliament. Hon. members will have seen in this morning's press, the announcement of the passing last night of another of our number, Mr. Harry Leader, the member for the constituency of Portage la Prairie.
It cannot be said that Mr. Leader's death was unexpected. For years past his health had been steadily failing, and before the end of last session he was obliged to give up his duties in parliament and return to his home.
Mr. Leader knew that he was suffering from the dread disease of cancer, but had hoped that the treatment he was receiving might prolong his life. Some time before the last general elections he announced he would not again be a candidate for parliament, but would devote the remainder of his life to furthering cancer research in whatever way he could. In the belief that he had made some progress towards recovery, Mr. Leader yielded to the wish of his friends and again became a candidate and contested the constituency successfully.
It is not without significance that Mr. Leader's death has occurred at a moment when there is under way a nation-wide campaign for the raising of funds to further cancer research and to combat by all known means the spread of this appalling disease.
Mr. Leader's death should speak even more strongly to the nation than any words or efforts he might have been spared to put forth had his life been further prolonged.
Mr. Leader was bom in Burnside, Manitoba, sixty-six years ago, in what was to become his home constituency-Portage la Prairie. In point of service he was one of the oldest members of parliament, having first entered the House of Commons at the general election of 1921. There are, I believe, only seven members of the present house who can date their first entry into parliament from 1921 or earlier. Mr. Leader's name gained special prominence in the general elections of 1921, at which election he defeated the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who at the time was prime minister. Mr. Leader himself was defeated by Mr. Meighen in the general elections of 1925. He did not become a candidate again until 1935, when he was reelected for Portage la Prairie. He was again reelected at the general elections of 1940 and 1945.
Mr. Leader was one of the best known of the western members of parliament. He entered this house and sat as a member of the Progressive party in 1921 until his defeat by Mr. Meighen in 1925. He was then absent from the House of Commons for ten years. In that interval of time he had, like the great majority of Manitoba Progressives become associated with the Liberal party, and when returned in 1935 took his seat on this side of the house.
For most of his life Mr. Leader was a farmer and will be remembered for his strong advocacy of policies which he believed would best serve the interests of the farming communities. He was a well-known figure as a breeder of pure bred cattle. A sterling independence and deep sincerity were outstanding qualities of Mr. Leader's character. In his passing the parliament of Canada has lost one who, throughout his life, had faithfully served the public interest in many fields of activity and who, in his death, has left a record of undaunted effort and heroic endurance.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Leader is survived by his widow, one son and two daughters. I know I express the wishes of all parties in the house when I ask that you convey to Mrs. Leader and other members of the family an expression of very sincere sympathy from all hon. members of the House of Commons.
The Late Harry Leader

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure members of this party would wish to be associated with the Prime Minister's remarks. For a quarter of a century, Mr. Leader was a personal friend of mine. He was born, lived his life and died on the Portage plains of Manitoba, one of the most fertile agricultural areas in Canada.
For forty years he was engaged in public life in one form or another, either in the municipal council or here in the House of Commons. During his service here he sought to do two things, among others; first, he tried to secure a better deal for that section of our economy which produces the nation's food; and secondly, in his later years, when suffering from a malady which all too often proves fatal, when he thought he had found in the researches of a medical man in Winnipeg a means by which the prevalence of this disease could in some degree be lessened, he sought to encourage cancer research and to spread the doctrines that improved nutrition might help prevent extension of that malady. His death yesterday is a further indication that this disease still has secrets from medical science. But I am one of those who believe that Mr. Leader's speeches were not made in vain, because in recent years we have learned that improved nutrition has a great deal to do with the prevention of disease and early death.
In the passing of Harry Leader, Manitoba has lost a good citizen and this house has lost a good member. We here are pleased to associate ourselves with the motion of sympathy moved by the Prime Minister.

maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext:
May I associate the members of the C.C.F. party in this house with the expressions of sympathy th'at have been heard. Like the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) I had known Mr. Leader for a number of years.
I knew him when we were associated together -in the old Progressive party; and while we sat in this parliament on opposite sides of the house Mr. Leader was one of the men for whom I and those associated with me had the very highest regard.
We have lost two members of the house " recently through this terrible scourge of cancer. I remember sitting in the gallery of the Saskatchewan legislature when I believe the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was leader of the opposition, and hearing one of his supporters, a doctor, who at the time was speaking of this dread disease make the statement that if that legislature represented an average group of persons in this country, of the sixty-five members

thirteen would die of cancer. In the same proportion, forty-nine members of this house might be afflicted with that terrible disease. Harry Leader performed a great service to this country, I believe, when he brought before this house as forcefully as he did the hope that something might be found to meet the menace of cancer. We shall long remember him as a fine son of Canada and as a splendid representative of that great class who produce the food of the country; and those of us who havei had personal association with him, in spite of any differences we may have had, will remember him as a fine and true friend.
On behalf of those associated with me, sir, I wish to join in the expressions of sympathy to his wife and family- in the great loss which they have sustained.

maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext: Mr. Leader was honest, sincere, independent, public spirited, and virile. As a member of parliament he was conscientious, industrious and effective. A genuine man of the soil, he was a consistent and progressive representative of men of the soil. Mr. Leader's death has occasioned a distinct loss to this house. The members of the Social Credit party join other hon. members in mourning his death and in extending sympathy to those bereaved by his passing.

maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was on my way
home for a long week-end when I heard of the death of my deskmate, Mr. Leader. I thought it my duty to return to Ottawa to say, in addition to what has been said of him already, that he believed in the brotherhood of man; that he was a great farmer and a great gentleman, with a big heart. I convey my deepest sympathy to his widow and children.

maintopic: THE LATE HARRY LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that Canada has not produced more men of the type, of the late hon. member, Harry Leader. His death is not only a loss to parliament but is a great loss to agriculture. His name will be remembered wherever Aberdeen Angus cattle are talked about, long after most of us have passed to the great beyond. Harry was a personal friend of mine for twenty-five years. I met him first as a fellow member of the United Farmers of Manitoba. We all appreciated his fine qualities, his honesty, sincerity and humanity. The greatest single quality which raised Harry in our esteem was his supreme courage. He fought against wrong wherever he found it. He always worked for what he thought was right, and championed

Lumber

Domestic Supply
the cause of the weak and the poor. He fought on courageously, though stricken with the incurable disease which has now taken him to his last home.
When words fail me in expressing my sentiments at a time like this I naturally turn to the ploughman poet of my native land, Robert Burns, who said:
An honest man here lies at rest,
As e'er God with his image blest;
The friend of man, the friend of truth,
The friend of age, and guide of youth;
Few hearts like this, with virtue warm'd,
Few heads with knowledge so inform'd.

speechtext:
['I believe I can say what I have Co say in the limited time left before six o'clock. I sometimes wonder, when I listen to different speakers, if we are not tending towards too much control. I had a great friend in the late Hon. James Malcolm and I remember one thing he said to me. "The more you interfere with natural laws, the more difficult it will be for government." There is a great deal of truth in that. You do not know where you will end if you start regulating everything.
I wish to direct the committee's attention to something which in my opinion is of current concern and importance. I will read into the record some remarks that have appeared in the Owen Sound Daily Sun-Times, on Wednesday, May 8, signed by W. E. Dickin, operator of an abattoir in that city. In this article he is pleading with people for tolerance and understanding with regard to the price of beef, and some of his remarks are important:
The whole situation is:	Can beef be sold at
twenty cents per pound ceiling price? My answer is definitely no. We are paying 12 to 12J cents per pound for cattle that dress 51 pounds to the hundred. The hide and other saleable parts are worth about $10. So any school child can figure out the loss on every bullock. Of course, if you can use common cattle it might be different, but this district demands and largely gets red ribbon beef.
He discusses other prices that are being offered and then says:
Bringing this to a close, what do we want or expect:
1.	Keep the price of all live stock up and encourage the farmer. He needs it badly.
2.	Compromise, Mr. Gordon and Mr. Gardiner, this once. We can all get together and say: This is our country. If mistakes have been made, let us learn by those mistakes. Again, I say, to one and all, compromise, and quickly.
I am trying to point out the immediate concern we should all have in this matter inasmuch as I believe that the farmers are facing a difficult task. When I listen to the speeches of hon. members and then contemplate the picture painted by the Minister of Agriculture I realize that if we are to encourage people to return to the land the picture will certainly have to be more colourful than the one we are given. We must face facts. In the county of Grey, which is largely an agricultural district, we produce large numbers of live stock. There has been-and I think this is a tragic fact

a

Supply-A griculture
shrinkage of two thousand in the rural population of that county since the last census. That means something. We must endeavour to make agriculture more attractive. In the same issue of the Sun-Times of Wednesday, May 8, the following appeared:
Keppel township council, meeting at Oxenden with all members present, instructed clerk Fred Carder to write or wire Donald Gordon demanding that the ceiling price of beef be raised or eliminated and that a copy of this demand be mailed to Hon. John Bracken, Garfield Case, M.P., and Findlay McDonald requesting their assistance.
There is something to justify the removal of the ceiling price from the products of the farm and ranch. You can fix the costs and other details of manufactured products but the farmer has to have some initiative to plant crops. In, a moment I shall refer to one of the things that has defeated that objective.
There is another item to which I should like to refer, namely, the position taken by an abattoir with regard to the ceiling price on beef. I hold in my hand a resolution passed by the Keppel township council with reference to the ceiling price on beef. It is taken from the same issue of the Sun-Times of Wednesday, May 8, and has to do with the local milk producers. What I am trying to do is to bring before the committee and to the attention of the administration a problem which is of current and immediate concern to agriculturists. This article is headed: "Local milk producers would halt deliveries if price not increased." The resolution is as follows:
Whereas we, the milk producers of Owen Sound district are experiencing increased production costs as never before through increased wages, et cetera and whereas the government has allowed increases to farm machinery manufacturers of 12J per cent, and whereas daylight saving time in collection of milk has made production more difficult and whereas we know that production costs are higher than ever before while retail price of milk is much lower than at many times in history, be it therefore resolved that all milk producers in this province vigorously protest and demand recognition in the way of increased price and that in the event of increased prices not being forthcoming we recommend that we discontinue supplies until arrangements satisfactory to producers are provided.
I have dealt with two important factors in agricultural operations, namely, the live stock and dairy producers. I come now to a letter which I received from one of my constituents, Mr. Carefoot. I might say that Mr. Care-foot is a well known breeder of short-horn cattle and draught horses and has exhibited his stock in some of the best rings in Canada. This is his story which I wish to convey to the committe so that hon. members will appreciate all the problems to which I have sought to relate my remarks. He says:
We as farmers are certainly getting it rough in the matter of labour. I am nearly sixty years
old. have hired men ever since I was sixteen, and this is the worst we ever had. You really cannot get help of any kind.
There are a few novelty farmers who make their money some other way and who can pay $80, $100 per month, get men, but their business from an agriculture standpoint is not paying.
The average farmer throughout the country who is paying for his farm, raising a family and buying equipment is the man we have got to pay attention to, for they are the real backbone of the country.
He goes on to say, and I think this is something that is really tragic when so many people of the world are crying for food:
I could name thirty men in this township who say if they cannot get labour at $50 per month, board and washing, they will simply just live on the farm and let the world go by.
As we know, the trend has been toward governmental paternalism, but it seems to me that it has led to a tendency to rob our people of the incentive to work, to rob them of their initiative.
This afternoon the minister spoke about two fine young Englishmen visiting Winnipeg. I cannot imagine our young men not visualizing the great challenge that this country offers; yet to-day we have young men who are capable of farming but will not do it. At the same time we have men like Mr. Carefoot offering to pay wages as high as $70 to $75 a month but unable to obtain labour. What is happening? About two weeks ago a group of young labour people, who were formerly the young communist group of Canada, interviewed various members of parliament. I had three young people who would be around twenty years of age interview me in my office in the parliament buildings. One young chap was from the farm. He isgetting out-of-work pay. I said to him: "Y7hy do you not go back to work on the farm?" He said: "The farm cannot pay me enough." I can say to these young people that while they might get 65 cents or $1 an hour in the cities or towns, the fellow on the farm has less opportunity to spend his money; he is in more healthful employment. I should like to see a great many of these young people return, because we shall live to realize some time that if we cannot make agriculture more attractive, induce our people to return to the land, to the good earth, as the hon. member for Assiniboia said, wages will not be as significant as they are at the present time. In other words, one might earn $1.25 an hour and still starve to death. I wish that labour, the farmers and others would realize that the basic economy of this nation depends upon the purchasing power of the dollar and not on the amount of money that is earned. I believe that agriculture still offers many attractions to young men to engage in that enterprise and feel secure in the days that are to

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction. On one or two occasions in the past he has answered questions with respect to the supply of lumber, but they do not quite cover the cases which have been brought to my attention in recent weeks from rural Manitoba.
I wish to ask the minister a question arising out of requests I am receiving with respect to supplies of lumber in rural Manitoba, requests which reveal what is said to be the most serious shortage in the history of certain of the towns there. Will the minister tell the
house what action the government is taking to meet the situation arising out of the shortages of lumber, particularly in small towns and rural areas in Canada, and what these areas may expect in the way of supplies during the next few months?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
maintopic: DOMESTIC SUPPLY IN SMALL TOIVNS AND RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, in referring to the most serious shortage of lumber in the history of those areas, is speaking, I presume, in a comparative sense only; because I feel certain that more lumber was used in Manitoba in 1945 than at any previous time in history. However, the supply is short of the demand. March and April are always the low points in the distribution of lumber, because, while the logs have been cut, the lumber has not yet been distributed from sawmills. The cut last winter was the largest in the history of Canada, considerably larger than in the previous winter, and I think that every yard can expect more lumber this year than it received last year. The additional supply is some 400 million feet more than last year.
The amount being retained for domestic purposes will be increased by the full amount of the increased cut, and I feel certain that by midsummer the supply of lumber in all parts of Canada will be much easier than it has been in the past.

maintopic: DOMESTIC SUPPLY IN SMALL TOIVNS AND RURAL AREAS
speechtext: Has any action been taken to curtail the export of lumber which is so badly needed in Canada?

maintopic: DOMESTIC SUPPLY IN SMALL TOIVNS AND RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
I have answered that question several times. I have said that lumber exports to our historic markets have been and are being maintained at their pre-war levels, and that the increased production in Canada is going into domestic use. I think the house will commend that policy. I think that countries which have relied on Canada in former years as their source of supply for their needs are entitled to receive that supply in post-war years as they did in the war years. We hope they can always depend on that supply. Canada is in a similar position in connection with its imports of commodities such as coal and cotton and a great many others. We rely on those countries which have in the past exported these supplies to Canada to look after the Canadian position in difficult times as well as in ordinary times, and I am happy to say that in general those countries have followed that policy. Canada is only doing for these countries what we wish them to do for us in following out our policy in the export of lumber.
Mr. ROSS (Sourish: There was a report in this morning's press that owing to shipping
Food Wastage

conditions in the United States much of the better grades of lumber intended for export to the United States are piling up in this country. I would ask the minister whether the controller could not divert some of this export lumber to lumber dealers in Canada until United States transportation difficulties are ironed out.

maintopic: DOMESTIC SUPPLY IN SMALL TOIVNS AND RURAL AREAS
speechtext: The controller is watching the situation very closely, but I would point out that the lumber exported is of different sizes and grades from domestic lumber and I doubt that it could be efficiently distributed in Canada. To distribute it in Canada would have no effect in the long run, because we have an agreement with the United States as to the quantity of lumber to be exported to that country, so nothing would be gained by taking the lumber now awaiting export.

Its chairman is Mr. Bradette, and it is open to any member at any time to ask that the committee meet together. The practice usually followed, is for a member who is desirous of having a committee meet to ask the chairman to call its members together. With regard to the meetings of this committee I would think that that would be the proper course to follow.
As to the second part of my hon. friend's question, which he was kind enough to send to me, namely that the committee should "immediately set about the consideration of recent world events which are bound to affect Canada's international position," that is I think for the committee itself to decide.
I am obliged to my hon. friend for sending me the question. Mr. Chairman, early this year the hon. member for Edmonton East paid a visit to Vancouver island. I hope that when the Minister of Fisheries is presenting his estimates the hon. member for Edmonton East will give us just as graphic a description of how he wrestled with a salmon as he gave us yesterday of how he wrestled with one of his sheep.
I notice that in his remarks he made some references to agricultural experts. Within a few miles of where he was staying this spring there is a dominion experimental farm where

there are a number of gentlemen who may well be considered experts in agriculture and horticulture. I want to take up a moment or two to-day to call attention to the difficulties under which these civil servants are working. They are doing an important service for the country and for the farmers and horticulturists who live in the vicinity of their farm.
The hon. member for North Battleford explained in considerable detail yesterday the activities of the Canadian Seed Growers Association. I know that these experts at the experimental farm have rendered very considerable assistance to the bulb growers, fruit growers and dairymen on Vancouver island, and yet one is forced to the conclusion that these experts have in the past received a remuneration hardly commensurate with their ability. I am informed that in the past their salary has been about thirty per cent less than that paid in some nine other professions in which people with similar qualifications - are engaged. Naturally these experts have to deal not only with the selection of seeds and the way in which fruit trees, bulbs and so on, are treated and protected against disease and the attacks of insects, but also with marketing conditions and other factors.
If we wish to attract to the agricultural service of the country the best type of our rural youth, we must give to those who enter that profession, an opportunity of making a reasonable livelihood, and we must also afford them opportunities adequate to retain them. I feel that in the past, owing perhaps to lack of understanding and appreciation, and to the exceptionally low salaries which have been paid, particularly to the younger men in the agricultural branch of the government service, we have run a serious risk of losing these men and of encouraging them to go elsewhere.
I offer these remarks merely for the purpose of calling the minister's attention to the need for stimulating interest in what I might term the professional agriculturists who have done such excellent work for the farmers.
I desire now to take up the theme of the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). I wish to refer to some of the statements he made in his speech yesterday. He said in part:

The next question I asked had reference to the number of veterans for whom equipment had been purchased. The number given was 1,127. The next question was with reference to the number who had made applications for equipment, and the figure given was 2,101. These figures surprised me; I thought there would have been many more. Then I looked to see how many veterans had been 63260-89
established on the land, and I found, as far as full-time farming is concerned, by March 31, 1946, that 5,132 veterans had been established under the Veterans Land Act throughout the whole of Canada. These figures struck me as amazingly small. I made inquiries as to how many veterans had already been demobilized, as I thought that would give me an indication of the number of veterans who were going back on the land. I found that from May 1, 1945 to March 31, 1946, over 500,000 veterans had been demobilized from the three services, and that prior to May 1, 1945, an additional 400,000 had been demobilized. Admitting that some of those veterans may have had dual discharge, because that is quite possible, the sum total cannot be less than something well over 800,000 men discharged up to March 31, as compared with just over 5,000 who had been rehabilitated on the land. Therefore fewer than one per cent of the veterans who have returned to this country have been established on the land.
Frequently we have heard of the great agricultural resources of Canada. I have always understood that agriculture was one of our basic industries. I have been told many times in the house that we had the most generous and far-reaching scheme for the rehabilitation of veterans that could be found anywhere in the world. Surely there must be something radically wrong with the position of agriculture in the economic set-up of Canada if only slightly more than one-half of one per cent of all the veterans who have been demobilized almost a year since the cessation of hostilities have taken up farming on their own under the generous opportunities which are offered under the Veterans Land Act. I do not know whether it is the fault of the agricultural policy of this country or of the general economic set-up; but it is obvious that these men who had the courage to face the enemy in the air, on the battlefields of Europe, on the high seas or in the merchant marine, for some reason or other think they have not a fighting chance of making both ends meet if they take up agriculture in this great agricultural country.
I do not believe that any amount of propaganda, any amount of explanation which may be given, or any attempt to show increases in exports of this kind or that, can blur the stark tragedy of these figures-one-half of one per cent of our veterans re-established into agriculture under the Veterans Land Act one year after the cessation of hostilities.

Speaking on this bill, as reported at page 4386 of Hansard of July 20, 1942, I said:
May I say at the beginning that if it were not for the fact that I have some faith in the future, and a hope that agricultural parity will eventually be established in Canada, I would not have been able to support the bill even in principle. In the great nation to the south of us, the United States, there has been parity between agricultural and other products for a year now, and under the Washington wheat agreement of June 27, 1942, signed by the Argentine, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, the representatives of these nations have recognized the basis of a parity price for wheat which will return a fair remuneration to the producers as well as being fair to the consumer. On the basis of these agreements, and having regard to what has been done in the United States,'I think we may hope that we are doing these settlers justice by establishing them on the land, because we hope that they will be able to carry on under parity prices, in the future at any rate. As I say, if it were not for that hope I for one could not have supported the bill.
I am prepared to admit to-day how illusory my faith was at that time, because under the increase in wheat prices announced in the United States the day before yesterday, and taking into account the difference in exchange, a farmer delivering his wheat in the United States will receive slightly over $2.50 a bushel, exactly double what the producer receives in Canada to-day. We have pretty well discussed the matter of dairy products, meat and other products. I repeated this declaration when we discussed the amendment to the Veterans Land Act bill last November. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about the matter under discussion. I do not wish to go into detail, because I agree with what the chairman has said, namely that in discussing this question we are more or less out of order. However there have been some remarks by hon. members to the effect that they come from the best farming con-63260-89J
stituencies in Canada; and then they proceed to tell us that nobody wants to farm there. My story is somewhat different from that. I think, in view of what has just been said, that I must live in what is really the best farming constituency in Canada, because the first veteran who came back and made application for a farm in that area referred the matter to me. Then, later on, to complete the story, I was informed by the land settlement board that in two years time he had paid back all the money he received from the government, and that he was not even waiting for eight more years to be paid the $2,300 to which he would be entitled under the act, in order to secure clear title. He paid it all back in two years and received his clear title.
I think it is important that when we are discussing matters of this kind we should not discourage men from going on the farms by telling all these hard luck stories. In spite of the fact that I do not believe they are getting all they are entitled to, the farmers to-day are making more on their farms than they have made at any other time in my lifetime. Young men who are going back to the farms under present conditions are not experiencing what has been suggested in the house. They are possibly going back under conditions which will probably make it more difficult rather than less difficult for them in the future-and not because conditions to-day are trying, but because they are a little better than they usually are on farms in Canada or in any other country. That is because there is a greater demand for food to-day than can possibly be supplied by all the farm operators in this and every other country.
This being so, conditions are at least as good as we can expect them to be for a long time for those who are now going on the land. But when the suggestion is made that at this stage young men are not applying to go back on the farms, particularly in western Canada, I think I can suggest a much better reason than the ones which have been offered up to the present. Those of us who have lived in western Canada in the last number of years, and particularly during the ten years preceding the war, can well understand why many young men and women who have served in the armed services or elsewhere are not now going back to the farms. One of them is, of course, the difficulty they experienced in the ten years immediately preceding the war. They may feel that there is a possibility of similar conditions prevailing at some future time, and they possibly feel that they would like to settle themselves somewhere else.
However, I do not think that is the reason which has developed this attitude in the
Supply-Agriculture

minds of most of them. Most of them know what to expect in western Canada; they were born and reared there. The only people who will ever make a success at farming in western Canada are those who know that for every four or five good years you have, you are going to have four or five poor years. One could not farm in that country were it not for the fact that it is comparatively dry. It is both too far north and too high up to farm under conditions where there would be any more moisture than falls there in an average year. Those who would operate successfully on a farm in western Canada must learn that lesson first. If they have learned that lesson, then it may be possible for them to make a success of farming on the prairies.
The fact is that in the last ten years before the war no one could make a living in western Canada, the reason being that the world was preparing for war. We could not have sold our farm products, even if we had had good crops in those ten years. We would have had a very difficult time. France did not want our wheat; Germany did not want our wheat; Italy did not want our wheat. They would not take it. The reason they would not take it was that in some instances they were preparing food in their own countries, producing it by synthetic processes in order that they might have it there, behind their own fighting lines, in a war which they all knew was coming, but which we would not believe was coming. Because we had those ideas in this country, we had people who were saying, "Oh, we are never going to have another war. Why do you prepare for war in this country? Why do you even think about it? There isn't going to be another world war." In other w'ords, we stuck our heads in the sand and let these people shut our food products out of their countries, thereby making it absolutely impossible for us to sell them. The result was that every boy or girl at home on his or her farm in western Canada just had to stay there. The farmers in this country do not do as the city people do, and I am not going to name any particular class of city people, because they are organized in a different way. In this country the farmer owns his own farm, or at least is trying to own it. He raises his own family on the farm. They are all part and parcel of the operation which is going on there. When their families are out of work because there is no market they do not turn their families out on the street to be kept by the state; they maintain their families themselves. Any person not gainfully employed on farms prior to this war was taken care of by the farmers, not by city councils or municipal councils or provincial governments or the
IMr. Gardiner.]
dominion government. Unemployment in that form was taken care of by the farmers themselves, with the result that thousands upon thousands of young men who should have been in universities or given courses to prepare them for life somewhere else off the farms did not have those opportunities. Why, anyone who knows farming in this country knows that only one boy can stay on the family size farm, and one of the neighbour's daughters. They constitute the new family heads who will remain on the farm; and if the farmer raises a family of four or five or half a dozen or ten children, the others have to find a living on some other farms, in business or somewhere else. Someone says it has been that way for a hundred years. It has always been that way where you have familysized farms, anywhere in the world.
So for ten years before this war began young men and young women were congregated upon the farms of this country because, during that period farming did not make it possible for them to obtain sufficient funds with which to secure the education or training they desired to permit them to go elsewhere when it became necessary for them to do so. As a result, during the war 400,000 of them left the farms and went into the services or. the war plants; and with them all gone we produced on our farms forty per cent more food than we produced in the years prior to the war when those people were on the farms. This proves, as conclusively as such things can be proved, that these young men were not gainfully employed on the farms during that period when they were not doing the things they desired to do.
The hon. member for Nanaimo says we have been boasting about the many fine things we are doing for returned men. The very fact that we have done fine things for them; the very fact that I am told that a man with certain qualifications, certain service and ' a certain family to be maintained can draw under these provisions as much as $10,000 to get himself an education, is the explanation as to why some of them are not applying to do anything else at the present time. That is an explanation of the fact that every university in this country is jammed to the doors with veterans, with as many more clamouring to get in, to take advantage of the provisions made by the government for men coming back from overseas to be trained and educated in the institutions of this country for the life that- is ahead of them. Before war broke out other countries were preparing for war, but we did not believe we should prepare for it. Therefore during the five or ten years before the war we did not take these men in and train them 'the way' we had to train

Supply-Agriculture
them while the war was on. We had to give them an education in order that they could fly as they ought to fly, in order that they might handle equipment as it ought to be handled, in order that they might lay out plans for the battles that had to be fought, and so on. We would not do that before the war, but during the war we had to do it. Then when the war was over we sent thousands upon thousands of them back into the educational institutions of our country to be educated as they should have been educated before the war started; so I am not going to blame any of them for not going back to the farms in the meantime.
On the last trip I made west, last Easter, I think I had a very good indication of why some men do not go back to the farms. I went into the dining car for dinner. A young man, or perhaps not so young either, in airforce uniform, sat down across the table' from me. He asked, "Have you an agricultural college in Saskatchewan?" I replied that we had. He asked if it was a good one, to which I replied that it was second to none, as far as I knew. Then he said, "Well, I think I will apply to go there." I asked what he was doing before the war, and he said he was teaching school.
I asked how long he had taught school, and he said seventeen years. I asked why he was going back to university now. His reply was, "Well, I got married rather early in life and I did not find it possible to complete a university education under the circumstances, so I had to teach." I asked what family he had; I have forgotten whether he said four or five, but he went on to say that under the provisions which had been put into effect it was possible for him to go and do what he had always wanted to do, that is, complete his education in an agricultural college, so he thought he would apply for admission to the agricultural college at Saskatoon.
There is no doubt in my mind but that thoughts like these are going through the minds of thousands of young men. Some day that man may go back to a farm. He is not so young now-[DOT]

If he knows anything about it he will say that those fellows do not know what they are talking about. If he does not know anything about it, he will say: I had better go and look somewhere else for a living. The fact of the matter is that in Great Britain only a small percentage of the people are on farms and the people who come here from the British isles are not accustomed to' farming. I would say that ninety per cent of the people of Britain do not want to farm and never did. Some of them when they come over here like to make money faster than they can on a farm and even if they settle on a farm are anxious to get away from it for a while.
Within the last forty-eight hours I met a delegation of real farmers who had a complain to make when they came in. Of course, that is what most people come here for, to make complaints and to get wrongs righted. In the conversation which took place a statement something like this was made. Twenty-five years ago we could go down the streets of our cities and towns and hire immigrants

who did not mind milking cows, hoeing sugar beets and doing other things that have to be done on a farm. There is no use in anybody going on the farm if he is not willing to hoe sugar beets, if he is not willing to milk cows, if he is not willing to feed pigs, and so on down the line. That is what has driven a large percentage of Anglo-Saxon people away from the farm. That is why so many farms in Canada are being settled by people who came from other than Anglo-Saxon countries.
If we want to keep our boys on the farm we have to preach a different kind of philosophy from what is being preached to-day in this house and elsewhere. We must preach the philosophy that there is nothing better or more worth while than producing food and clothing, the two things that are necessary for all of us. If farming, producing the things we need the most, is not considered one of the best of all professions or trades, or whatever you like to call it, there is something wrong with our way of thinking.
It is all very well to get up here and say what a wonderful class of people our farmers are, how fine they are; but just take your pencils and put down $1,600,000,000, which is the highest cash income the farmers of this country ever took in for three years' work- that was in the last three years-and divide it by 800,000. What do you get? It gives you $2,000 as the average cash return on a farm in Canada in the best three years we ever had in this country.
I go down to Toronto and a man tells me, as he did on one occasion: There is no reason why the farmers should not be the wealthiest people in Canada. I asked him why, and he said that someone had ninety acres just outside Toronto and they took $40,000 off that land every year. I said, "What are you talking about?" He said "They are taking light hogs off the market in Toronto, feeding them out on that land and then turning them back on the market when fit, and they took in $40,000 a year by doing that". He went on to say that there was no reason why every farmer in Canada should not do that. I said to him, "There are two very good reasons why it cannot be done,"-and hon. gentlemen would be surprised to know who this man was. He gives us advice about running this country. I said to him, "There are two very good reasons, and the first one is that if every farmer in this country produced that many hogs every year he would not be able to find a market for them, even at possible Chinese rates of return. The next reason is that there is not enough feed produced in Canada to feed a fraction of that number of hogs if every farmer was producing them."
I said to him, "You are not talking about a

Supply-Agriculture
farmer; you are talking about a feeding lot, where a man takes the hogs, buys the grain, puts the hogs through his feeding plant and turns them back on the market. That is not a farm; that is not farming." Then I know of other cases: these cases are typical. Whenever you go into a certain part of this country and ask somebody to take you out and show you a farm, I know where he will take you. And I know that the man who owns that farm never lived on a farm in his life. I know that he got the first money with which he started his agricultural pursuits running an evangelistic campaign. I know that the next basis of the fortune which went into that farm came from race horses, and that the land was purchased as a result of that. It is a very fine farm, and most people who go to see it come away thinking that the owner is the type of farmer we have in Canada, that those are the type of people we have on farms in western Canada. I hear it said that they go to California every winter, or they go somewhere else in order to enjoy themselves; they do not farm; they work only a few months in the year. I have heard statements something like that since this debate started. These may be very fine people but they are not farmers.
I had the privilege only this'morning of having verified something which I thought I had learned when I was in Europe recently. I have heard-I won't use the term I was going to use, but I will say-I have heard a great deal of buncombe about farming in some countries which are a long distance away. I always had the idea that at least fifty per cent what I heard had. no basis in fact, but was based on what one is shown by propagandists for a thing. So when I was in Denmark last January I hopped out of the plane and into a car and I said, "Nobody knows I am in this country at all, nobody would know who I am if they did know I was here, so just show me a few farms". A young air force chap ran me around to half a dozen farms and I went in and took a look at them. I was never more surprised in my life than when I went into these farms. I have never seen on any well-run farm in Canada as poor cows as I saw there. I would not have the same kind of horses on my farm as I saw on some of theirs, and the chickens were as mixed as any flock of chickens you ever saw on any farm anywhere in the world. So I thought, well, there may be something wrong with the picture I had drawn for me of farms in Denmark. Only this morning I had the opportunity of having breakfast with a gentleman who made the remark that he had written a book on this matter some years ago, having been sent over by the government
to investigate farming conditions in Denmark and elsewhere. I said, "What did you find?" "Well", he said, "I thought what I might see around Copenhagen might not be typical of the rest of the country, so we did not go to Copenhagen first. We just slipped in up over the mainland; we did not say anything to anybody, and we visited a number of farms before they knew we were in the country." "Do you know", he said, "that their farms are not any better than the back concession farms in Ontario? They are much the same type, operated in much the same way"; and he went on to tell me that when he drove into a certain place he was invited to dinner, that the mother of the family was out in the garden or out in the field, down on her knees, weeding sugar beets. He said ^he was dressed in clothing which looked very much like what we call gunnysacks. "What we had for dinner", he added, "was tapioca and one or two other foods which we would think very common on our tables in this country." I mention this in order to emphasize that this was the picture I found when I was there, but I was, not sure of it. But he said that when the officials got hold of him they did not take him to places like that, but to places like the one of which I have been speaking and which you can find in this country too- quite a number of them-outside of Toronto and Montreal and probably Ottawa and other cities. I think we should toot our own horn instead of suggesting that our boys found things so much better elsewhere that they will not farm in Canada.
Too many people in this country do not know the farmers' condition, and too many people who don't know talk about it. As I have indicated, farmers in this country have had in the past three years an average cash income of about 82,000 gross, and out of that they must pay at the present time, if they want to get a man at all, about $100 a month, which is $1,200 a year. If anybody can tell me how a farmer who has to pay that much for help can pay much income tax, I Should like to know how he is going to do it.
I thought I had to say that some time, and this is just as good a time as any to say it. We have been talking a lot about general matters, and a considerable number of those who have been on their feet have said that we ought to have more money for agriculture. I think I said at the beginning that we had increased the expenditures in every division, and everyone who has mentioned it at all has said that we ought to have even more. Well, I quite agree, but I have not been able to convince everybody else of that. But if I have convinced the committee of it I should like
Supply-Agriculture

hon. members to do one thing: let us pass one item and get on with voting the money we have been allowed.

speechtext:
That, too, is interesting, but the minister would have done better not to raise the question of what he and I have been accustomed to having.
I think it was also unfortunate that the minister spoke of visiting the people of Denmark and came to the conclusions he did, considering that they were under German occupation and that many of their best breeding herds were completely destroyed. I spent two weeks in Denmark a number of years ago before the country was overrun by the enemy.
I admit frankly that every farmer in Denmark has not a perfect herd, but the Danish people have earned a reputation all over the world for excellent breeding stock and producing a 
high quality dairy product. They have held the British market for years, and I should not be surprised if they made a bid for it again. I do not know how many farms the minister saw during his brief visit, but it is most unfortunate that a Canadian Minister of Agriculture should make comparisons of the kind as a result of such interviews as he had.
Every session I have taken advantage of this item to recommend to the minister that there should be a certain reclassification of salaries for the personnel in his department. But before proceeding with those remarks I should like to pay a tribute to him for a valuable international service which his department has recently rendered. I have a letter from P. S. Quan, who is an engineer attached to the department of irrigation, ministry of agriculture and forestry, in China. He recently spent three weeks in Canada studying irrigation and soil surveys work here. He visited the experimental station at Sum-merland, the irrigation projects in the Lethbridge district and the P.F.A.A. office in Regina. He writes to me:
The admirable work done by your department-*
I may explain that he was drawing his conclusions entirely from his association with these three branches.
The admirable work done by your government and the intelligence and diligence of your farmers gave me deep impressions of the battle of food production. My Canadian trip was a most profitable one not only from the point of view of giving me a very good picture of developments in your country but also of giving me much information for our future developments in China.
I suggest that if the minister, from time to time, could find ways and means for promoting that sort of communication it would have a much better effect than the sort of contribution he made this afternoon with reference to Denmark.
I might also express thanks to the minister for a recent appointment that has been very well received in all parts of Canada, particularly the west. I refer to the appointment of Doctor K. W. Neatby as director of scientific services. This gentleman is one of the most distinguished graduates of my own alma mater, the university of Saskatchewan, and I am sure that everyone who knows him and knows the work he has done is glad to have him back in the work he is so well trained to do.
When I was discussing these estimates a year ago I said that in my opinion the personnel in the Department of Agriculture did not receive as adequate compensation as the personnel in other departments, or persons outside the government services. I may have

Supply-A gricul ture
strange ideas in connection with these matters, but it is my opinion that the Department of Agriculture is as important as any other department of government. The minister has referred to the fact that the people who do scientific work in his department are probably as well paid as farmers. That possibly is true; but I think it should be the goal of the minister to see that those who work on farms receive the highest possible income, or at any rate that they have a fair share of the total national income. Likewise, those who work under his supervision in the government service should have a fair share of the amount spent for all services.
I do not think we can solve both problems immediately, but I do not think we should wait, to make adjustments in the civil service, until we have solved all other problems in the wider field of agriculture.
Last year the minister answered a question regarding the number of employees holding the bachelor's degree and receiving certain salaries. One receives less than $1,000; 287 receive less than $2,000; 358 receive less than $3,000; and only 96 receive over $3,000. There are sixty with master's degree reeciving less than $2,000; 113 receiving less than $3,000; and forty-seven receiving over $3,000. With the Ph.D degree there are ten receiving less .than $2,000, forty-one receiving less than $3,000, and, sixty-two receiving over $3,000.
I have never argued that because a man has a college degree he is entitled to an income that places him in a position of advantage over his fellows, but I imagine that most of the employees in the department holding degrees have come from farms. If one boy stays on the family farm and continues to develop it, even if his income is only the average of $2,000 over the whole nation in good years, while another boy goes to university, spends four years taking the bachelor of science degree, another two years receiving his master's degree, and a total of eight years until he receives his Ph. D., and if the latter has to pay off his debts and maintain a decent standard of living he should receive an income higher than the amounts paid to so many of the personnel of the Department of Agriculture.
Last year the minister argued that in his opinion the salaries in his department compared very well with those in other departments. However, checking over the public accounts, I find that the assistant deputy minister in the Department of Agriculture receives $4,800 a year, whereas the assistant deputy minister in the Department of Munitions and Supply receives $9,000. I am not
acquainted with either of these gentlemen, but I assume both have important responsibilities.

speechtext: I think the comparison could be made to better advantage with some other department, because the Department of Agriculture is permanent, whereas the other is only temporary, doing a temporary job, and considerations such as go with permanent employment do not go with it.

subsubtopic: MINISTERIAL ARRANGEMENTS DURING PRIME MINISTER'S ABSENCE IN LONDON
speechtext:
I realize that. I know that what the minister says is quite true, but when you have a man coming in from private industry and working alongside a civil servant who is better qualified and does a more responsible job at half the salary, you are bound to have friction. In the Department of Agriculture we have a relatively short list of men receiving $2,400 a year or more, whereas in the wartime prices and trade board alone I find that there are ten pages giving salaries of more than $2,400, many receiving $5,000, $6,500, $7,000, $8,000, and so on. The same goes for the Department of Munitions and Supply.
I submit that those who have been doing such important work in these scientific fields require a return that is a great deal higher than they have ever received. Last year when these estimates were up I referred to the annual pay of some of my class mates who were in university twenty years ago. Doctor Broadfoot receives $2,880. He was a brilliant student, one of our popular undergraduates. He went to the university of Minnesota and took his doctor's degree and now, after nearly twenty years, he receives a salary of $2,880. There is Mr. Russell, who has done outstanding work in the field of rust, who also receives $2,880; and there is Mr. Mead, who receives $2,400. These are three of my classmates who have all had upwards of twenty years' service and they are getting less than $250 a month. I maintain that this sort of compensation to industrious and capable civil servants is not good enough.
I was interested in an article in the Journal of the Professional Institute of the Civil Service of Canada, and I find that this problem has been agitating the civil service for many years. Back in 1922, shortly after the present Prime Minister took over his responsibilities, he was disturbed by the salaries prevailing in the civil service. However, the wheels of government move slowly, and it was not until 1927 that a special committee of the cabinet finally forwarded a directive to the civil service commission to make a survey of compensation rates paid to professional and scientific employees, with instructions to report
Supply-Agriculture

their findings to the government. That was in March, 1927. A year later certain recommendations were presented and they involved the spending of aprpoximately $750,000 more than was being spent. Those were the days, I may say in passing, when the question, "Where shall we' get the money?" really stopped things. Nothing happened. Then about a year later, on April 16, 1929, a royal commission was established with the late Sir Edward Beatty as chairman and the late Doctor Walter Murray, of the university of Saskatchewan, and Sir George Garneau as members * of the commission. They made a careful study and they came to certain conclusions. One of their comments was as follows:
We have been especially impressed, however, by the slow rate of advancement observable among officers with from eight to twenty years of seniority. Many of these officers at a time of life when financial responsibilties of a growing family are apt to be heavy, have not yet reached a scale of salary which can be regarded as adequate, even for a decent subsistence. If their professional competence is not open to question, then they should be provided with opportunities for advancement which will at least enable them to pass on to their children the same educational advantages which they themselves have had.
But the recommendations they proposed required an additional $750,000 annually. The Minister of Finance of that day, the Hon. Charles Dunning, was completely stumped by this problem. I understand that Mr. Dunning is being honoured by the university of Saskatchewan. When we think of the problem of finding $750,000 in 1930 to meet injustices which had existed in Canada for many years we wonder why we could not find so little money when during the last four or five years we found so much for war purposes.
In this article there is a reference to the sort of treatment we have meted out to civil servants. It referred to Doctor Saunders, the man who gave Canada Marquis wheat. There can be no argument at all that his discovery has meant hundreds of millions of dollars to the people of this country, and yet we are told that in the estimates for the year ended June 30, 1905, the late Doctor Saunders was receiving the princely sum of $1,250, or little over $100 a month.
A good deal of publicity has recently been given to the development of rescue wheat. I understand that the principal work has been done by A. W. Platt, of the Swift Current experimental farm. His discovery is also going to mean millions of dollars to the wheat producers of this country; yet Mr. Platt's name does not even appear in the public accounts among those receiving $2,400 or more. I understand that he is receiving
(Mr. Nicholson.]
$1,800 a year, to support his wife and four children. I have also been informed that he has been offered a salary of $5,000 to go to the state university in Kansas, but because of his loyalty to this country and his hope that some day a measure of justice will be granted to civil servants like himself he has declined the offer to leave Canada. But I do not think it is fair to expect scientific workers who are doing this kind of work to continue in Canada indefinitely. I cannot see any good reason why this country which has raised so much money to prosecute a war cannot demonstrate now that we can adjust these grievances.
In the December issue of the Institute Journal there is a table showing a comparison of salaries paid to agricultural scientists in Canada, the United States and Great Britain. I am sure this comparison will be of interest to the committee and I shall read it. In the lowest grade Canada compares favourably with Great Britain. In grade 1, our range is $1,800 to $2,400; in the United States, $2,552 to $3,278; in the United Kingdom, $1,210 to $2,200. I might say that in these comparisons the United States dollar was taken at $1.10 and the British pound at $4.40. In grade 2, Canada, $2,400 to $3,000; United States, $3,278 to $4,004; Great Britain, $2,420 to $3,300. In grade 3, Canada, $3,000 to $3,300; United States, $4,004 to $4,730; Great Britain, $3,420 to $4,840. In grade 4, Canada, $3,300 to $3,600; United States, $4,730 to $5,698; Great Britain, $5,280 to $6,160. In grade 5, Canada,	$3,600	to	$4,200;	United	States,$5,698 to $6,622; Great Britain, $7,040 to $7,920. Grade 6, Canada, $3,900 to $4,500; United States, $6,853 to $7,777; Great Britain, $8,800. Grade 7, Canada, $4,500 to $5,100; United States, $7,892 to $9,047. Grade 8, Canada,	$5,100	to	$5,600;	United	States,
$9,625 to $10,780. There is a note appended which states that in the United Kingdom they have various salaries in these high ranges from $9,900 to $11,000. Since this table was prepared I understand that there have been increases in the United States for all those getting less than $1,200. There has been a twenty per cent increase on salaries up to $1,200, a ten per cent increase from $1,200 to $4,600, and a five per cent increase above $4,600. I have also been informed that there was a resolution passed in the house of representatives approving a further flat increase of $400 over the whole service, but the senate was not prepared to go quite that far.
In one of these journals a list is given of the new members who have joined the veterinary group of the institute. Checking over the public accounts, I found that these men who have had a long and costly college

Supply-Agriculture
course are receiving salaries of $250 a month or less. I hold in my hand a copy of a brief that was prepared for the investigation in connection with health insurance by Doctor J. S. Fulton, director of animal research in the university of Saskatchewan. In his brief Doctor Fulton complains that compensation to graduates of veterinary science has been so low that they have not been able to attract a sufficient number of young men adequately to care for the health of animals and the supervision of meat and milk offered for public consumption. I know that most of the veterinarians listed here are engaged in the health of animals division. I have seen some of these men at work in the abattoirs. I consider that their work is of a responsible nature. It is not easy work. I can see no reason why these university graduates are not as important to the people of Canada as are the salesmen for Canada Packers or the Swift Canadian Company. It casts a serious reflection on our whole economic set-up when graduates in veterinary science find that if they give up the practice of the profession for which they were trained and look after cats, dogs and canaries they make a handsome living; whereas if they go out to the country to look after the health of cattle, horses and sheep they find it difficult to make a living.
In his brief Doctor Fulton points out that at the time it was prepared there were only forty-five qualified veterinary surgeons in the whole of Saskatchewan, which has a horse population of 830,000, a cattle population of 1,602,000; a dairy cow population of 467,700; a swine population of 1,325,400 and a sheep population of 410,000, not to mention a poultry industry with an estimated $20 million involved, returning to the producers $9,976,000. The whole point of my argument is that in my opinion the compensation provided by the Department of Agriculture for those who are well qualified in the various branches has not been comparable with the returns in other departments of government, and certainly not comparable with the returns-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with keen interest to what has been said by the minister. Each time he speaks he treats us to some first-class oratory. However, on this occasion I do not find myself in agreement with him when he appeals to the committee to pass the first item in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, so that we may get along more quickly. There is no one in the committee more anxious to proceed with the business than I am; but when I am convinced we are going in the wrong direction I cannot see any good reason for hurrying. In view of government policies announced in the past few weeks in connection with increases in the price of farm machinery, and an increase of three cents a gallon on gasoline, I am firmly convinced that the decontrol policy of the government respecting agriculture is not a satisfactory one. To my mind it is more important that we place some facts before the government in the hope that it may reconsider its decontrol policy for agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture has made an appeal that we adopt the philosophy of urging people to go back to the farm. I can agree with him but assure him that my appeal, my philosophy, will be from a different angle. Rather than speak from a capitalist philosophy, I shall speak from the philosophy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.
In the past few weeks we have heard from some of the ministers some emotional appeals for rationalization. I, for one, feel the time has come when we should stick to facts, figures and statistical data if we wish to legislate properly for the people of this country.
When the Minister of Finance was making his appeal, in justification of the 12^ per cent increase in the price of farm machinery, he said that we must have faith in the wartime prices and trade board, on the ground of its war-time performance. That is not good enough to-day when we are trying for all-out production to feed the starving peoples of the world, when we are fighting for peace at home, and to establish an economy where we can live in decency in a time of peace, rather than just in a time of war. It is of the utmost importance that we consider carefully all the issues involved in any policy. My contention is that this problem cannot be solved individually.

Supply-A griculture
Agriculture is linked with other problems in the country. The future, the prosperity-yes, and the happiness of the farmers, the workers and the everyday people are indivisible. So, too, are their troubles interdependent. After having sat here last session and so far this session it seems to me that the elephants of monopoly, if I may call them that, are having another party. During the war these people were making tremendous profits; in other words, they had a party, and they came out of that with huge amounts of money. _ I remember the evening the Minister of Finance announced in the house an increase in the ceiling on farm machinery. I was sitting in my seat, and it seemed to me he was making a purely emotional appeal to this house. For a while I thought he was giving us a real
sob-story in behalf of the farm machinery companies of this country; but when I looked down at my desk I saw some financial statistics for a number of companies taken from the Bank of Canada statistical summary, October-November, 1945. I should like to put this table on Hansard without taking time to read it. If I have permission of the committee I shall do so; otherwise I intend to read it into the record. Have I your permission, Mr. Chairman?

I have just tabled reports showing the profits some companies have made during the war. I want to go farther and prove to the Minister of Agriculture, if I can, that this implement price increase at this time is completely unjustifiable. I have here the report of the select special committee on farm implement prices and distribution of the legislature of Saskatchewan, dated March 27, 1939, from which I desire to quote in regard to the price structure. This is what I find at page 10, speaking of farm machinery companies:
Early in 1936 the companies announced an increase of price in farm implements amounting to 4-4 per cent as found by the Ottawa committee. It was this particular increase, announced after a substantial reduction in the tariff from 25 per cent to 12J per. cent, that gave rise to the Ottawa inquiry. Despite a further reduction in the tariff to 7J per cent and despite the findings of the Ottawa committee that this increase was not justified and that the prices of farm implements had been, over the years 1913-36, too high, despite, too, a definite finding that there was an excessive markup over cost on cream separators and repair parts, and that the prices of these should be particularly and substantially reduced, this committee finds that none of these findings were given effect to, and that, in addition, further price increases occurred in 1937.
Further on, the report has this to say in reference to labour costs:
Between 1930 and _ 1933 the Massey-Harris company put in operation a ten per cent decrease in wages paid in their plants. In 1935 the company restored two and a half per cent of this decrease and since then has restored the balance of seven and a half per cent, thus reestablishing the same scale as was' in force in 1929. It can, therefore, be clearly seen that

the increase in the price of implements between 1929 and 1939 is not attributable to higher wage costs. In 1929 the I.H.C. binder sold in Begina for $283, and in 1939 for $324.75.
Carrying that a little farther, Mr. Chairman, I find in the Journals of the House of Commons for 1937 tables showing that the cost of an eight-foot binder in 1913. was $84.96. The price to the fanner was $165 and the net sales realization. $123.03, or a profit of a little over 28 per cent. In 1935 the total cost was $128.29; the price to the farmer was $265.50; the net sales realization was $187.23. and the profit was $58.99, or almost 46 per cent. There is an estimated backlog of farm machinery in this country to-day amounting to around $200,000,000. If we take the profit per $100 of cost, according to this table appearing at page 435 of the Journal, we find that these machine companies, in filling their backlog of farm machinery will make a profit of around $140,000,000. The government has allowed certain increases in the price of steel, and it has also been argued that labour is partly responsible for the increased prices of farm machinery. I have here a table showing that profit, not labour, is the cause of high prices for farm machinery. This is taken from The C.I.O. News of September 10, 1945. It refers to a United States federal trade commission report, and has this to say:
The idea, which is common among farmers, that labour costs are the reason for the high price of farm machinery is completely exploded by the study, which shows that labour costs range from only 5-9 to a maximum of 14-6 per cent of the price the farmer pays for his machinery.

Supply-A gricul ture
It goes on to say that this federal trade commission report takes a combine selling for $638. The labour costs were only $46.43, or 7-3 per cent of the price paid by the farmer. Materials such as wood, steel, iron, fabric, rubber and so on cost $174.27. Counting the work of mining ore, cutting the timber, and so on, plus the factory work, the labour cost was $221. This leaves $417 to be accounted for in factory overhead, manufacturer's and dealer's margin, freight, manufacturer's distribution and dealer's discount. It goes on to say:
The retail dealer's margin is 19-1 per cent and the manufacturer's margin is 13'4 per cent compared to the manufacturing labour cost of 7-3 per cent.
I could go on, and give more figures showing that this price increase is not justifiable, but I wish to point out here that the government allowed an increase in the price of gasoline. I have here a report by Mr. L. G. Reynolds in relation to the commission on price spreads, which has this to say:
For many years the Imperial Oil has refined most of the gasoline sold in Canada, and this concern "fixes" prices for the industry. Imperial is the "price leader" and the other companies -follow. Each dealer is generally bound by contract to take his gasoline from only one company, and the dealers are controlled by tacit agreement among the companies to withhold supplies from price-cutters.
The companies have set the price of gasoline at a level that provides a wide profit margin. This has led to limited competition among the companies, not in price but in sales-extremely wasteful sales practices, and serious duplication of personnel, storage facilities, retail outlets, et cetera.
A survey by the royal commission on coal and gas products in British Columbia, for instance, found that there was one gas station for every 48 cars in Vancouver as compared to one for every 114 cars in Seattle, Washington. The commission concluded that in most towns in British Columbia one-half or more of the stations could be eliminated with no loss in convenience to the public.
There we have the situation of this government allowing price ceilings to rise without thorough investigation of the effect on the Canadian economy and considering whether it is justifiable. I have received a letter from Mr. Brown, president of the Cooperative Implement company in which he says that this policy of the government has accentuated the need for cooperative control of farm implement prices. Since this is reflected in the Canadian economy and is bound to have serious repercussions all across the country I would recommend that the government consider seriously using the Combines Act and that it should not be satisfied until a thorough investigation has been made of the big machine companies in Canada.
I remember distinctly when the Windsor strike was on last year that, according to press reports, General Motors refused to allow government auditors to see their books to ascertain whether labour's demands for wage increases were justified. Therefore I suggest that the government make a thorough investigation of the prices of farm machinery to determine scientifically whether a price increase is justified.
I am in agreement with, decontrol but not the type of decontrol which, on the one hand, satisfies the demands of people like these big machine companies and at the same time stabilizes the prices of farm products. The whole subject must be investigated on a scientific basis.
I have listened with interest to the Minister of Agriculture, for whom I have a great regard. I think he knows his department perhaps as well as any minister in the government. I was much interested in hearing him refer the other night to the principle of the ever-normal granary and to stability of prices. We in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have constantly advocated over the past years the ever-normal granary, and unless the minister is just paying lip-service to this principle of the ever-normal granary-
