speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. But the remarkable thing is that the minister is advocating the ever-normal granary now when we have no grain and are scraping the bottom of our bins. But you cannot do it in that way. If you are to have the ever-normal granary you must take the good years and the lean years too. I stated in the house last year that we should adopt such a policy in Canada.
A report has -been handed in to the provincial government of Saskatchewan by a commission appointed under the former Liberal government in Which it is stated that the chemurgic use of farm products in western Canada was not feasible in view of our lean and good years. It is true that we have lean and good years. If we have 500,000,000 or 600,000,000 bushels of wheat to-day, under our present system we call it a surplus, but I say that if we have 1,000,000 bushels properly stored throughout the prairie provinces it should be like money in the bank.
I am a farmer and I do not think I can be classified among those to whom the minister referred as knowing nothing about farming. I feel a responsibility in the matter of what should be done in this crisis which we are facing to win the peace. The minister said
Supply-Agriculture

that he did not know how the farmers were going to pay income tax out of an income of $2,000, which was the average annual income of Canadian farmers in the best three years in our history. I might say to the minister that I cannot see how the farmers are going to pay 124 per cent increase in the retail price of farm machinery. There is a nigger in the woodpile in this whole business of farm machinery. When I was home at the Easter recess the local dealers had a meeting in Regina and were told by one of the head men of the implement company that they were lucky to get any machinery at all because the company had overseas commitments which would take them many years to fill. There should be an investigation of this whole question of farm machinery, so that our farmers who during the past five or six years have built up a backlog of requirements during that period of controlled purchasing power on account of the war may be able to get a decent supply of farm machinery. If it is not forthcoming, the government should do something about the matter.
The Minister of Agriculture referred to some of the stories that are going around about people leaving the farm, many of whom are not going back. I am alarmed at the urbanization which is taking place in this country, and if there is anything we can do, and should do, it is to get our people back on the land. This trend of people leaving farms and going to the cities seems to me one of the most disastrous things facing Canada. People who live on the land have a sense of values perhaps lacking in people who do not know the feel of the good earth and have never known what it is to grow something. I am disturbed at the decrease in our rural population. The Canada Year Book says:
Of the farm land already occupied in Canada, only 39-40 per cent of it is actually in use, and for the past several decades there has been a steady trend towards a smaller farm population. During, the relatively prosperous decade of 1921 to 1931 a net total of some 350,000 people shifted from rural to urban areas. During the five-year period 1931-36 the prairie region actually lost population equivalent to 63 per cent of its natural increase, and during 1936-41 it lost all of its natural increase and 16,000 besides. In other words, the prairie provinces have been sending a surplus farm population elsewhere rather than absorbing population from other areas on the land. The rural areas of other provinces have had the same experience to a smaller degree.
There are reasons for that. I was in Fort William recently and spoke there, and in a visit around the city with the mayor of Fort William we went to that very fine building which was erected by the Canadian government to house the girls who were working in

the Canada Car factory. The city of Fort William had taken possession of that building and were making it into two and three-room suites, because they had a housing problem. As we went through one portion of that building, which cost around $300,000, and I saw all the bathtubs piled up in a large room- there seemed to be dozens of them there-I remarked that I had seen more bathtubs in that one room than in all the Saskatchewan farms I had visited. That indicates one reason why our boys and girls do not want to go back to the farms. I should like to read to the committee, and I hope the Minister of Agriculture will listen, in view of his intimation that groups like ours are going around and spreading propaganda which was frightening people away from the farms, a statement contained in one of the government's own publications introducing Canada to British war brides. The title is "Not luxurious-no, not quite." This is What it says:
Though usually comfortable, a Canadian farm home is not luxurious. You have only one chance in five of having electric light in a farm home, which means you must use coal oil (paraffin) lamps. You have only eight chances in one hundred of finding any sort of plumbing in a farm home, outside facilities taking its place. Six farm homes out of ten have radio (wireless), three have telephones, and nearly half have motor cars. One-third of Canada's farm homes have none of these conveniences. A considerable number are in need of repairs.
As I said, this is from "Welcome to War Brides", an official publication of the government. So that it is not only members of our group who may be accused of spreading propaganda which will deter people from taking up farming.
I have travelled from here to the province of Saskatchewan a matter of seven times in the last few months, and in doing so I met with a number of veterans. To-day veterans are trying to make up their minds what they are going to do. I .feel that I know something about farming, not everything; but at least I have learned the hard way and, as the minister has stated, there is no better life than life on a farm, provided that one can make ends meet and have a, decent standard of living and not be loaded down with debt so that mortgage companies and farm implement companies are hounding you day in and day out. But when a veteran speaks to me about going on to a farm and asks me what I think about it, I am afraid that conscientiously I cannot tell him that he has an even break. We find to-day that land values have gone up, and not only so, but there have been increases in prices of farm machinery and gasoline. Right there we have two strikes against the veteran.

Supply-A griculture
Again, in the last year, although the government recognizes the need of some sort of stability for agriculture, there was a ceiling put on wheat for export. It is true that a floor was put under it too, but we never applied a quota to the amount which might be delivered. So that I think we have yet to go a long way to convince the veterans that agriculture in Canada has anything like stability. If in two or three years we in this country return to peak production, and European countries likewise go back to full production, we may be again faced with the problem of having several hundred million bushels of wheat on our hands. Veterans ask me, if that situation should take place, what will happen; are we to return to low prices and perhaps be unable to handle our live stock? Because, Mr. Chairman, we have not as yet any long-term agreements which will ensure decent prices for live stock. When I think that this government has seen fit to give only $6,000 as a maximum for veterans starting on the land, and now has allowed a 12% per cent increase on machinery, I do not see how, unless these veterans are first rendered unconscious or are forced by exceptional circumstances, they are likely to go back on the farms. Let me point out that to-day you cannot get a small tractor for less than $1,500, and if you go to one of these sales of second-hand implements you will probably pay $2,200 or $2,400 for an old one, as they did in Yorkton. A small combine costs $1,700, and a truck costs $1,200. So that there, for three major pieces of machinery, you have a total outlay of $4,700; yet the veteran is allowed only $1,200 for farm machinery and $4,800 for land. How in the world is he to rehabilitate himself? The fact is, of course, that the veterans are just not going back on the land.
However, in my constituency there are quite a number of boys who have tried to save some extra money during their period in the services, and this is what they have found. When they go to the board they are investigated and inspected to find out if they are physically fit and otherwise capable of going on a farm. Often they find that it takes months for them to get the first interview. Then the property on which they wish to go has to be inspected. I took this matter up with Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan, and I should like to pass this on to the minister and ask him what he can do about this matter. It is in regard to hastening the inspection of the lands of these veterans who want to settle on the land. One person who was in the forces for five years, and has a family of five, was delayed three months before getting an interview with the board. After he was passed
he went back to try to have his land inspected; it was in the district where he wanted to farm; the owner was retiring and had this land for sale. The situation was-and it is a typical one-that unless he made a down payment he would probably lose the property. It might be said, well, he could get a farm some other place. But that is not a satisfactory solution, for this reason, that a good many people want to go to the districts in which they lived before; they have their hearts set on a certain piece of land; they want to operate a certain farm. In the particular case I mention the veteran made an initial payment of $480 to hold the land, but when he tried to get it inspected there was nothing he could do about it, as the board advised him, until the following year.
I wish to point out that after men have served for five or six years and have come home and want to start up, something should be done to hasten their rehabilitation. I have heard that under the present set-up, and at the speed with which applicants can be interviewed and the land inspected, it will take years before the veterans are properly established, and it is not satisfactory simply to tell these men that they had better get something temporary. I spoke to the premier of the province asking whether they would be prepared to cooperate with the federal government in expediting the inspection of the land, and Mr. Douglas assured me that he would be ready to use the agricultural representatives of Saskatchewan, of whom there is a considerable number, in this work. I would appeal to the minister to do something about this matter.
There is just one other recommendation I would make to the government. We need to plan scientifically if we are to win the peace. We have had enough of the emotional appeal in this house, and if we are to have in Canada an economy that will be best for all the people it will have to be worked out on a scientific basis.
In conclusion, I would say this. Holding the views I do, I realize quite well the interdependence of the farmer and the common people. Nevertheless I courteously and as strongly as I can urge the minister and his colleagues to set up negotiated prices so that the cost of living and the cost of production as well as all other costs shall bear a fair relationship and that we may thus have production for use rather than for profit as the mainspring of our Canadian economy.
May I in closing quote from the C.C.F. manifesto:
The future prosperity of the Canadian people requires the fullest development of Canadian agriculture. In the past the Canadian farmer
Supply-Agriculture

has not received a fair share, of the national income. Agriculture, in the main, has accumulated huge deficits because farmers have received less than their cost of production. No modern industrial nation can afford poverty in any section of its people. The farmer is a consumer, as well as a producer. Farm people are entitled to the same standards of health, housing, nutrition and education as other sections of the Canadian people.
I believe the Minister of Agriculture himself, while in Saskatchewan, made a statement to the effect that at the time we went on to rationing of beef we had not shipped any beef out of Canada. That is an important statement, because in the first years of the war we started to put pay checks into t*he pockets of the workers so that we had a market for beef, butter, pork and cheese. While, therefore, we are concerned about foreign markets I suggest that we should see to it that there are no hungry children in this country and that everyone has all that he wants to eat and has a full stomach.

speechtext:
I believe I can say what I have Co say in the limited time left before six o'clock. I sometimes wonder, when I listen to different speakers, if we are not tending towards too much control. I had a great friend in the late Hon. James Malcolm and I remember one thing he said to me. "The more you interfere with natural laws, the more difficult it will be for government." There is a great deal of truth in that. You do not know where you will end if you start regulating everything.
I wish to direct the committee's attention to something which in my opinion is of current concern and importance. I will read into the record some remarks that have appeared in the Owen Sound Daily Sun-Times, on Wednesday, May 8, signed by W. E. Dickin, operator of an abattoir in that city. In this article he is pleading with people for tolerance and understanding with regard to the price of beef, and some of his remarks are important:
The whole situation is:	Can beef be sold at
twenty cents per pound ceiling price? My answer is definitely no. We are paying 12 to 12J cents per pound for cattle that dress 51 pounds to the hundred. The hide and other saleable parts are worth about $10. So any school child can figure out the loss on every bullock. Of course, if you can use common cattle it might be different, but this district demands and largely gets red ribbon beef.
He discusses other prices that are being offered and then says:
Bringing this to a close, what do we want or expect:
1.	Keep the price of all live stock up and encourage the farmer. He needs it badly.
2.	Compromise, Mr. Gordon and Mr. Gardiner, this once. We can all get together and say: This is our country. If mistakes have been made, let us learn by those mistakes. Again, I say, to one and all, compromise, and quickly.
I am trying to point out the immediate concern we should all have in this matter inasmuch as I believe that the farmers are facing a difficult task. When I listen to the speeches of hon. members and then contemplate the picture painted by the Minister of Agriculture I realize that if we are to encourage people to return to the land the picture will certainly have to be more colourful than the one we are given. We must face facts. In the county of Grey, which is largely an agricultural district, we produce large numbers of live stock. There has been-and I think this is a tragic fact

a

Supply-A griculture
shrinkage of two thousand in the rural population of that county since the last census. That means something. We must endeavour to make agriculture more attractive. In the same issue of the Sun-Times of Wednesday, May 8, the following appeared:
Keppel township council, meeting at Oxenden with all members present, instructed clerk Fred Carder to write or wire Donald Gordon demanding that the ceiling price of beef be raised or eliminated and that a copy of this demand be mailed to Hon. John Bracken, Garfield Case, M.P., and Findlay McDonald requesting their assistance.
There is something to justify the removal of the ceiling price from the products of the farm and ranch. You can fix the costs and other details of manufactured products but the farmer has to have some initiative to plant crops. In, a moment I shall refer to one of the things that has defeated that objective.
There is another item to which I should like to refer, namely, the position taken by an abattoir with regard to the ceiling price on beef. I hold in my hand a resolution passed by the Keppel township council with reference to the ceiling price on beef. It is taken from the same issue of the Sun-Times of Wednesday, May 8, and has to do with the local milk producers. What I am trying to do is to bring before the committee and to the attention of the administration a problem which is of current and immediate concern to agriculturists. This article is headed: "Local milk producers would halt deliveries if price not increased." The resolution is as follows:
Whereas we, the milk producers of Owen Sound district are experiencing increased production costs as never before through increased wages, et cetera and whereas the government has allowed increases to farm machinery manufacturers of 12J per cent, and whereas daylight saving time in collection of milk has made production more difficult and whereas we know that production costs are higher than ever before while retail price of milk is much lower than at many times in history, be it therefore resolved that all milk producers in this province vigorously protest and demand recognition in the way of increased price and that in the event of increased prices not being forthcoming we recommend that we discontinue supplies until arrangements satisfactory to producers are provided.
I have dealt with two important factors in agricultural operations, namely, the live stock and dairy producers. I come now to a letter which I received from one of my constituents, Mr. Carefoot. I might say that Mr. Care-foot is a well known breeder of short-horn cattle and draught horses and has exhibited his stock in some of the best rings in Canada. This is his story which I wish to convey to the committe so that hon. members will appreciate all the problems to which I have sought to relate my remarks. He says:
We as farmers are certainly getting it rough in the matter of labour. I am nearly sixty years
old. have hired men ever since I was sixteen, and this is the worst we ever had. You really cannot get help of any kind.
There are a few novelty farmers who make their money some other way and who can pay $80, $100 per month, get men, but their business from an agriculture standpoint is not paying.
The average farmer throughout the country who is paying for his farm, raising a family and buying equipment is the man we have got to pay attention to, for they are the real backbone of the country.
He goes on to say, and I think this is something that is really tragic when so many people of the world are crying for food:
I could name thirty men in this township who say if they cannot get labour at $50 per month, board and washing, they will simply just live on the farm and let the world go by.
As we know, the trend has been toward governmental paternalism, but it seems to me that it has led to a tendency to rob our people of the incentive to work, to rob them of their initiative.
This afternoon the minister spoke about two fine young Englishmen visiting Winnipeg. I cannot imagine our young men not visualizing the great challenge that this country offers; yet to-day we have young men who are capable of farming but will not do it. At the same time we have men like Mr. Carefoot offering to pay wages as high as $70 to $75 a month but unable to obtain labour. What is happening? About two weeks ago a group of young labour people, who were formerly the young communist group of Canada, interviewed various members of parliament. I had three young people who would be around twenty years of age interview me in my office in the parliament buildings. One young chap was from the farm. He isgetting out-of-work pay. I said to him: "Y7hy do you not go back to work on the farm?" He said: "The farm cannot pay me enough." I can say to these young people that while they might get 65 cents or $1 an hour in the cities or towns, the fellow on the farm has less opportunity to spend his money; he is in more healthful employment. I should like to see a great many of these young people return, because we shall live to realize some time that if we cannot make agriculture more attractive, induce our people to return to the land, to the good earth, as the hon. member for Assiniboia said, wages will not be as significant as they are at the present time. In other words, one might earn $1.25 an hour and still starve to death. I wish that labour, the farmers and others would realize that the basic economy of this nation depends upon the purchasing power of the dollar and not on the amount of money that is earned. I believe that agriculture still offers many attractions to young men to engage in that enterprise and feel secure in the days that are to

come. I am glad that the Department of Veterans Affairs is making it as attractive as possible for veterans to engage in that type of work, since they are accustomed to the outdoor life.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday an interesting debate occurred on this very bill. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank), speaking on the principle of divorce bills in general, suggested the setting up of some sort of organization or special court to handle the divorce cases which came from the province of Quebec. In support of his proposition he put a few facts before the house, and I say that they are true. But I am afraid that some misapprehension prejudicial to the province of Quebec might result if certain other facts were not placed before the house.
The hon. member said, "There is no general divorce law in the province of Quebec." That is a well known fact. Then the hon. member continued, as reported at page 1190 of Hansard:
It has developed since some time past that whenever adultery is committed in the province of Quebec and the outraged husband or the outraged wife wants to do anything about it, he or she comes to the parliament of Canada and asks the parliament of Canada to pass a special law, among all the other statutes with which it has to deal, giving her relief as it is called, in the event of a female spouse coming forward, from continued association with her adulterous husband.
That statement was also true, but it might be misunderstood or misinterpreted.
It is not a fact that the civil code of the province of Quebec does not provide relief in the case of adultery. On the contrary, the law of Quebec provides for the separation of the consorts; it provides for the settlement of their property; it provides for the custody of the children; it provides for the payment of alimony. It even provides for an ever-possible reconciliation. As a matter of fact, the Quebec legislation has almost the same immediate effect as a divorce bill, the chief difference being, as everybody knows, that neither of the

parties legally separated can marry again during the lifetime of his or her consort. That kind of relief the Quebec legislation does not provide.
The immense majority of the population of Quebec on account of its religious belief does not give special consideration to such relief- just sympathy, I should say. The hon. member is very much concerned with his own personal situation as a member of- parliament when he says:
It seems to me, sir, that it is not a proper part of the duties of the parliament of this nation to be continually considering, in the midst of its important business, these trivialities.
He is right again. But in 1867, by the British North America Act, divorce was attributed to the federal jurisdiction because some people believed in it. They insisted on it, and it was so attributed against the opposition of Quebec. It is an historical fact that Quebec refused categorically to accept it, although it was pertaining to civil rights.
The hon. member now finds that he has an ever-growing and almost impossible problem to settle. I really sympathize with him; and all the Quebec members are in the same predicament of dealing with these trivialities.
Respecting his project of the setting up of some extra-territorial organization to deal with divorce, I have no comment to make, except that it will probably come into conflict with every rule of domicile and court jurisdiction extant.
I humbly submit to his consideration that he find himself a practical solution. I would agree with his suggestion that-
... we make some sort of declaration that this ' sort Qf petition will not hereafter be entertained, and that petitions of this sort cannot be received by this parliament with any chance of being acted upon.
I would agree with that if it would be of any utility. Personally, I almost feel like washing my hands of the whole business. There is a moral to be drawn from the speech of the hon. member, and it is this: Sometimes, just once in a while, somebody should listen to someone from Quebec.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of what the hon. member has said, seeking to justify the position of the people of Quebec, the situation continues to stand in this house as it has done for many years. I support the suggestion made the other evening by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) when he sought to suggest some method of relieving this house of parliament of the onerous duty of dealing with divorce. I am satisfied that if proper attention and thought

Private Bills-Divorce
were given the matter by the lawmakers of this land, some equitable disposition of the problem could be found. I do not for one moment believe that it is impossible for the House of Commons to arrive at some position which would be satisfactory to all parties.
I for one object again in this session, as I objected in the last, to the time of parliament being wasted by having to handle such business as this. However, I have noticed that several times in the debate the suggestion has been made that these are trivialities. I take strong objection to the use of that word in this connection. I would say they are tragedies of human life; they are not trivialities by any means. I believe that they are real tragedies, but that they should be settled somewhere outside the House of Commons.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the last sixteen years I have listened to discussions of this kind at nearly every session of parliament. It is not a new problem. Divorce comes under federal jurisdiction; but because one or another of the provinces wanted to set up divorce courts of their own, it was done and at the present time there are divorce courts in eight of the provinces. Quebec is the only province with no such court. Hon. members know why that is so. In principle we are against it. Last year when I spoke on this question, the moment I stepped out of the house one of my friends stopped me and said, "You should not have gone that far. Do not try to impose on Quebec something that they do not wish or do not like or do not believe in because there is a minority in Quebec that will want to have divorces as the years go on." I reminded him that when Ontario proposed to establish a divorce court the Catholics protested, but the law was passed.
I am broad-minded on these matters, but in principle I am against divorce and I am going to do my utmost to try to make the getting of divorces as difficult as possible. A complaint has been made in the other place that there are too many petitions for divorce this year, but if you consider the number of cases coming before the other place and this house you will find that it is only about one-fifth of the cases being brought up in this good province of Ontario. I clipped the

following report from one of the Ottawa papers on May 8, knowing that this discussion would come up. This is what it says:
Ontario divorce figures believed to be record
Provincial authorities said to-day that Ontario had so many divorces in 1945 that they are recheeking the figures to make sure they are correct. Tentative figures show an all-time high of 1,939 compared with 1,510 in 1944 and 960 in 1940.
I have the utmost respect for those who believe in divorce. I do not believe in it myself. If we believe that the future of our country is based on the family, divorce is not the way to bring about the conditions we desire.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU
speechtext: You do not keep families together by refusing divorce.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU

That is a matter of opinion, and I respect the hon. member's.
What gets under my skin is this. Every session some hon. member says that this procedure is not the right one. But if hon. members would go into the divorce courts in the provinces they would see that the evidence is taken in just the same way as it is in the other place, and I believe that in the other place we have men who are as experienced as any judges in hearing these cases and deciding on the evidence. The evidence is prepared and presented in the same way. If some cases are not prepared well, let me say that I can recall cases right in this capital city in connection with which a man was sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary for fixing up the evidence given before the court to obtain a divorce. We may find the same thing here. But it is tiresome to hear hon. members year after year saying that there is one way out of it, namely to give the provinces jurisdiction in divorce.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU

If we give jurisdiction in divorce to the provinces, the provinces that believe in divorce can have their divorce courts; but in the province of Quebec, where they do not believe in divorce, they would have no divorce court and there would be no divorce at all. The other suggestion was to have a court in Ottawa, perhaps the exchequer court, with special jurisdiction in divorce cases. The province of Quebec is a part of this country. There are over 3,000,000 people in that province. We want harmony; we want unity; we want respect for other people's opinions; but we also request from this parliament respect for what we believe. I think we are right. Many people think we are wrong. But, after all, we are not asking for more than a few hours of the time of parliament where for sixteen years I have listened to nonsense being talked hour after hour. Always there are the same arguments and the same replies, and what I am saying to-night has been said in this house year after year. The arguments and replies will not change as time goes on. I have been present at the committee in the other place, and the procedure there is just the same as in the courts. The only argument that might be made here is that we spend too little time in giving our decision on the evidence presented. If you do not wish to read the evidence, you are just taking the recommendation from the
other place, and it is not a bad thing at times to base our judgment on what they decide.
I hope I have not said anything that displeases those who do believe in divorce, but I am simply telling the house what I have heard in my own province since I was a boy. I think we should bear with the present system for a while yet.

Mr. Speaker, I think I shall have to agree, like the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), with the position taken by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and also with the members on my left.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) said that he has listened to an awful lot of nonsense: spoken in this house.

If what the minister has said to-night is not nonsense, I am afraid that it is very contradictory. We do not say that we believe in divorce any more than we say that we believe in theft or any other kind of misdemeanour that may bring persons into our courts. But we do recognize the necessity for divorce. Among Roman Catholics I understand that marriage is a sacrament which cannot be dissolved, but the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Belzile) has told us that the procedure for annulments in Quebec is practically the same as divorce in every way except that the parties cannot remarry.
What I rose to say, however, is this. If divorce is within the jurisdiction of this parliament-and that must be true because we have exercised jurisdiction for many years- it cannot be beyond the power of parliament to find a way of providing divorce courts for the people of Canada, no matter where they live. Every civilized country so far as I know has divorce laws. They have ways by which persons, when they find they cannot live together, can separate. That does not contribute to immorality; it diminishes immorality, and I think that is how we should look at the matter. A broken home does not take place with the divorce; the home was broken before the divorce became necessary.
I suggest that we try to find a way of dealing with this important question, and I say again that this parliament having jurisdiction in the matter can create some other way than by this parliament passing divorce bills.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU
speechtext:
I am one who in this house
usually speaks only when he is spoken to, and I have endeavoured to adopt that as a policy since I came here as a new member last summer. I rise to agree in some respects with the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). I do so by reason of the fact that I have arrived at that conclusion by another route.
If we look into the history of divorce we shall find that the province of New Brunswick had machinery for divorce from as far back as 1791; in the province of Nova Scotia they also had it, although not quite as far back as that, but they had it prior to confederation. It will be remembered that at the time the fathers of confederation met in Quebec and the Quebec resolutions were adopted, it was agreed by the parties that marriage and divorce should come within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament; and again when the London resolutions were framed it was agreed that marriage and divorce should come within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. As a result, the British North America Act was enacted, and since that date marriage and divorce has been under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. We quite realize that in Canada we have different races, different religions, and different nationalities. The church to which the Minister of Public Works belongs happens to be the Roman Catholic church, and for them marriage is one of the seven sacraments. The church to which I belong happens to be the Anglican church, or Church of England, and although marriage is not regarded as a sacrament, divorced couples are not allowed to be remarried by the Church of England in Canada.
It may seem strange that a bachelor should rush in and make some comments on the question of divorce. But my reason for speaking this evening is to say that I have followed these discussions both before I was in the House of Commons and since, and so far as I can see at the present time there is no way that you can get around the presen! system. I am sure there is no desire on the part of anyone to impose upon the province of Quebec a court which the majority of the
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
people in that province do not want. At the same time it should be remembered that from the days of confederation in 1867 marriage and divorce have been within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, and if you will look in your statutes for the year 1868 you will find that the first divorce case came before the Senate and the House of Commons at that time; it was reserved for the Queen's pleasure; it was sent to England; and finally the act divorcing the couple, who were from the city of Montreal, was affirmed.

So we see that since confederation there have been certain persons in that province who desire the right of divorce. Here is the situation: the majority there are definitely opposed to It; the minority, on the other hand, have had that right ever since 1867, and the first case was heard in 1868. From that date on I believe you will find if you check the figures that there was one _ case each year; then the number gradually increased to ten; and now you all know that the figure this year is 330 or thereabouts. .
At the present time we have that situation. We have this committee of the senate dealing with these divorce bills. I have had some experience in divorce courts and, looking over the proceedings as I have seen them carried on here, I feel that the work done by that senate committee is just as careful as it is done in many of our courts.
One of the speakers last week remarked that in many cases there was collusion. That is quite possible, and I do not say that it is not so, but it is also quite possible that there is collusion in many cases which come before the courts of the various provinces.
Therefore as I say, the situation is that the majority of people in the province of Quebec do not wish divorce; a minority in that province have had the right ever since 1867 to come to ^his parliament for divorces. I am sure there is no desire on the part of anyone in this

I have several times taken part in discussions of divorce procedure in this house, and I had no intention of taking part in the discussion to-night, but the trend of the debate has more or less compelled me to rise and say that I want to support those who believe that we should find a method different from the one which is now adopted for the consideration of divorces. I think that this is a matter for a court rather than a parliament of this description or the hon. gentlemen who occupy the other place. I think that a judicial body can look into the applications more carefully than they can be looked into at least by this house; and, after all, you and I as members of this house have to take the responsibility for the dissolution of these marriages. That, I suggest, is one of the gravest responsibilities which we have to assume, and one which we ought not to assume unless we know upon what grounds the petitioners request divorce and warrant us to grant the divorce. I doubt very much if there is more than a very small minority in this house who read the proceedings upon which the applications are based and upon which we have to vote.
Like the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) who just preceded me, I happen to be a member of the Anglican communion. While it is true that the church to which we belong does not believe in divorce, in the last few years there has been a liberalizing of the views regarding divorce until to-day in Great Britain the Anglican church will remarry the innocent party in a divorce case.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU
speechtext: Not in Canada.

maintopic: JULIANA EDMONDA ISABELLA FERDINANDA BECQUAERT DE BEAUJEU
speechtext:
That, I think, is something which might be remembered in this house. But what I was going to say is this, that with the large number of unhappy marriages, my personal view is that it is the greater crime to keep two people tied together living in what has often been described as a 63260-90
hell, than it is to dissolve that marriage. I think it is worse for the children who are brought up in such a home than it is to allow those children to be looked after by, we will say, the innocent party, upon direction of a judge in a proper court of law where all the evidence has been submitted and reviewed. I think, too, that to keep a man or woman tied indefinitely to a chronic alcoholic is to make life a hell, and that cannot lead to a higher morality in any country. I believe that where there is venereal disease on one side it is again a hell to keep the innocent party tied in such circumstances.
To-day we are at the conclusion of a great war, and I remember what a padre told some of us-I believe the Minister of Public Works was one of the party-who rode with us from Glasgow to Edinburgh, of the condition which he found in 1941 among a percentage, small it is true but still a percentage, of the men overseas. He told us on that occasion that when the war ended we would be faced with a problem. Well, this parliament is faced with a problem and we are not doing anything in particular to cope with it.
Those of us who know something about the conditions to which some of the men who served overseas have returned realize that this parliament is faced with a problem. It is true my hon. friends in the province of Quebec who belong to the Roman Catholic church believe that under no circumstances should divorce be permitted, and I agree that so long as they are members of their church they should abide by its'discipline. I am not complaining of their view because of their religion. I am suggesting to them, however, that there is in the province of Quebec a minority which does not accept that doctrine, and I believe that the rights of minorities should in all respects be recognized and protected, just as we wish to protect the legitimate rights of our Roman Catholic compatriots in the province of Quebec and elsewhere.
I suggest to my hon. friends also that the minority in that province have a right to have their views considered. No one is compelled to sue for divorce, but where individuals believe that divorce is warranted and it does not conflict with their consciences, surely that minority has a right to the exercise of a conscientious conviction in respect of the relief to which it believes it is entitled.
If the province of Quebec does not-and I do not think it will-establish a court of itself, as the other provinces have done, to which these cases may be referred, then I suggest, since we were asked a few minutes ago what the solution is to be, that there



Canadian Wheat Board
should be a federal court to which applications could be made, to which a minority could go if the majority in that province does not believe that its conscientious objections would permit it to establish a provincial divorce court.
I wish to plead with my hon. friends from the province of Quebec to look at the matter in the light in which I am trying to view *it, not as a believer in divorce but as one who believes that a suffering minority in any province should have the right to divorce if it feels the need of it and if divorce does not violate its own convictions.
I suggest, therefore, that what should be considered is the establishment of a court or the naming of a court already established. I do not know whether that is possible. I have heard it suggested from time to time that once of the courts, such as the exchequer court, might be given jurisdiction in these matters. I do not know what court it should be; but if we have not a court that could give speedy and proper consideration to these matters, then I think it is incumbent upon parliament to see to it that people who are tied together to-day in what is sometimes a living hell are given a proper opportunity for relief from the position in which they find themselves.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

With these exceptions the increase in the Department of Agriculture is less than any other department of government.
Most people across Canada realize the importance of agriculture, and most people expected an increase in the expenditures of the Department of Agriculture. But if we are ever to come to the point where we shall have balanced budgets in this dominion we must save somewhere. With the terrific increases in other branches of government to as high as 44-8 per cent in some cases, while in agriculture the increase is only 11-4 per cent, it does not seem that agriculture is getting its fair proportion when one considers its importance. Agriculture has always taken a back seat, and it appears from these figures that it will continue to do so. I wish the minister success in convincing other members of the government of the importance of agriculture to this country.
Most hon. members will have some idea of the present butter situation because of having had to do without it for some time in the House of Commons restaurant. The reason for the scarcity is quite obvious to me if not to other members. The price of milk for butter and cheese production in the United States is practically double that which is paid here. The United States buyers, therefore, can well afford to pay the high prices they are paying for dairy cattle. This price range is so high that it is almost impossible for a man to refuse it. Just last week a United States buyer paid as high as $185 for a grade first-calf heifer. Is it any wonder then that the number of dairy cattle exported to the United States up to May 2 of this year was 16,332, while the total in 1945 was only 11,452? If this government would allow a reasonable increase in the price of dairy products, thereby enabling the farmer to make a reasonable profit for the extra work involved in dairying, the sales of these cattle to the United States would shortly show an appreciable decrease.
Yesterday the minister mentioned an increase in milk production. Yes, there has been an increase in milk production, but not anywhere near the proportion that the consumption of whole milk has risen. I could name a number of instances in my own riding where large producers were forced out of milk production because of lack of labour. Then, again, I could cite dozens of cases where men who previously had sent milk to concentrated milk plants, powdered milk plants, and cream to creameries have now, with this huge increase in the consumption of whole milk, the opportunity for which they have been waiting for years, that of getting into the *whole milk trade. That is happening all across
(Mr. Charlton.]
Canada. It is not only happening in my own riding. It is a general condition, and I contend that that is the reason for the decrease in the production of butter, which is obvious from the figures the minister showed us yesterday with respect to Ontario, particularly. In 1939 the production of butter in Ontario was 88 million pounds. That was the high year. In 1945 it was reduced to 77 million, a difference of 11 million pounds.
We all realize that Ontario is the most highly industrialized province in the dominion, and we would expect the consumption of whole milk to go up there more than it has in other provinces. I might say that that increase has been quite a bit better than 50 per cent in Ontario. So that we would naturally expect that that milk had to be stolen from some other branch of the industry. The fact that creamery patrons have taken much less for milk separated and going to creameries is an obvious indication of where it would be lost. I contend it is impossible to control prices and stop inflation during an obvious scarcity. There are always people who want the article badly enough that they will gladly go out and pay black-market prices. They will continue to do so, so long as any product is in short supply, notwithstanding the fact that many officials of the department at Ottawa claim that there is very little black-marketing in Canada.
Take beef cattle, for instance. Reported marketings thus far this year are 52,839 head short of the same period in 1945. The minister would not suggest that beef cattle production has gone down that much. Where are those cattle? The very fact that retail butchers are paying higher than ceiling prices for beef carcasses, and still making a reasonable profit-or they would not be doing it-leads one to the belief, as was stated by the minister at page 1246 of Hansard that "by having the price levels determined by competition" is the proper method of correcting the situation. Another method is by removing restrictions on butchers killing their own beef and pork, commonly known as the quota system, and thereby releasing the strangle-hold which the large packers have on the industry.
Under present price controls I understand the retail butchers get a little better than $40 spread on a 600-pound carcass of beef. I leave it to the judgment of hon. members to. say whether that is a fair spread or not. I contend that the price to the retailer could go up two cents, without increasing it to the consumer.
It would appear that most of the terrific spread between producer and consumer prices

is caused by the consumer demand for service, i maintain that it is very unfair for all consumers across this country to have to pay for the service that a few expect. If certain consumers demand these extra services, why should they not pay for it themselves, without making a blanket charge to all?
This brings to my mind two striking examples. Two years ago I happened to be in a hardware store in the city of Brantford talking to the manager, when a lady telephoned in for an eleven-cent pane of glass. The manager later told me that she lived almost two miles from the store, but she wanted it delivered immediately. I think all hon. members will realize that the cost of delivery would be two or three times the cost of the glass.
Something similar occurred when I was visiting at an apartment house in Toronto. About ten-thirty or eleven o'clock at night the people I was visiting wanted to buy a brick of icecream. They telephoned the drugstore, and that 25-cent article was delivered- I do not know how far. But somebody has to pay those delivery costs. It is not always the consumer who pays it; most often it slaps right back in the face of the producer.

I should like to answer a few of the questions raised by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I was not at all surprised by the line of argument presented in the earlier part of his speech, in view of the fact that my hon. friend has not always advocated the policies he is now advocating.
The situation which has existed in connection with agriculture estimates is one which is very well understood by most hon. members. The suggestion was made that the present government, and more particularly the present-minister, is to be criticized for not obtaining a larger proportion of the treasury funds for expenditure upon agriculture. I should like to refer the hon. member to the records of the past. During the period the Liberal government was in office between 1921 and 1929-30 there was a constant increase in expenditures upon agriculture until the provisions made in the last year the Liberals were in office were for the highest expenditures upon agriculture that we had had up to that particular time.
In 1932-33 the estimates for agriculture were reduced from a previous $11,000,000, to which amount they had been built up under a Liberal government, to $8,660,000. The next year they were reduced to $8,203,000, and the next year they were reduced to $7,395,000. I took over the department in 1935-36, and by 1936-37 the estimates had been increased to $15,553,000, or double what they had been in the last complete year that the preceding government had been in office.
I was invited to Toronto during the third year that I had had the privilege of administering the affairs of this department and I was met with a full page in the Toronto Globe and Mail. I have just forgotten the heading that they used to run at the top of that page, but at the bottom was a coupon which could be cut off and sent to the government at their suggestion without any expense to the treasury because it was considered to be government business. We were getting those on our desks in the House of Commons at the expense of the Post Office Department. The protest they made on that occasion was that I had provided for the enormous expenditure of $20,000,000 on agriculture. That criticism was carried on by the opposing party of that time right down to the day that war opened. This year the comparable expenditure with 1936-37 is over $17,000,000.

This group would maintain that the standard of living of the people of Canada throughout Canada, agricultural, industrial and all other workers, ought to depend upon the capacity of this country to produce and deliver goods and services, and upon nothing else. May I turn for a moment or two to the prices affecting beef. Our whole structure of prices as it affects beef ought to be reviewed and revised most carefully. Once more, I am not imputing any of the blame for these prices to the minister, and perhaps those administering those prices have done the best they could. But it is my duty as member of parliament for my constituency to tell the committee what the effect has been upon beef production in my riding. The prices on beef during the years 1942 to 1945 inclusive have not been conducive to the maximum beef production in Canada. In 1942 the prices destroyed the confidence of producers in my constituency. I do not believe that confidence has ever been thoroughly restored, and what happened in the last six weeks has given another serious blow to confidence in the production of beef. In fact, beef prices in 1946 would appear to be a deterrent to full and confident participation by feeders in beef production in the future. Between
11,000	and 12,000 beef are estimated to be in my constituency ready to be marketed by the middle of June. If the men who are feeding those beef between now and the marketing of beef in the middle of June lose money on the beef, there will be many a plate in Can-ade next year without a beef steak which would have been supplied with one had prices been more wisely managed.
It must be understood that when men put money into beef in the fall and then put good money into feed of various kinds, and devote long hours of hard work coupled with great anxiety in the production of beef, and then because of price manipulation are forced into a loss where they had counted on a gain, they will react just as members of this house would. Their attitude will be, once bitten, twice shy.
I have in my hand a letter from a prominent beef feeder in my constituency, dated April 17, 1946, Lethbridge. From that letter I will read one short paragraph:
The fact is that feedlot cattle cannot be produced at present ceiling prices. To discount this fact or the importance of the feedlot in the production of meat tonnage is unjust and is wilfully or ignorantly out of accord with the facts.
Those are pretty strong words and they come from a well-informed man who has great 63260-91
experience and who to-day is finishing in the neighbourhood of from 5,000 to 7,000 cattle.
So much for the objections or criticisms I have to offer. I wish to protest against the increase in agricultural machinery prices to be paid by the farmer. I wish to protest against the increase in gasoline prices. I wish to protest against the undependable manipulation of beef prices. I am not prepared to enter into the matter of determining scientifically exactly what is wrong at the present time, but something is wrong and it must be made right.
What can be done in the future? I believe hon. members have put their finger on the difficulties. It is easy to say what is to be done; the problem is how to do it. In the first place, prices must be made equitable in agriculture. In the west we are using very commonly among the farmers the expression " parity prices." No one has ever defined "parity prices" with complete satisfaction, but generally the idea is quite clear that the farmer should be able to get enough from his production to enable him to buy a fair amount of the produce of other people who produce goods for him.
That principle must be discovered and must be applied throughout the country. There must be parity prices as between agricultural products and the goods which^farmers buy. Then there must-be stability of prices. It must be obvious to anyone that when the price of potatoes, let us say, is likely to be down to 35 cents a hundred one year and up to $1.25 in the next year and down again to 80 cents, no one can possibly participate with confidence in the production of potatoes. And potatoes would be only one of the com-_ modities.
Surely, if agricultural implement manufacturers can have a stable price for their product over a series of years, the farmer should be able to have a stable price for what he produces. This principle of stability must be established and maintained. The government has gone a long way in the endavour to establish that, and it is worthy of commendation for it. But much more must still be done, and I am sure the minister does not disagree with that. His problem would be the very question I have raised: how to do it, how to get the money to do it.
There is another matter that must be established and that is dependability of markets. If I am in the potato business and I propose to raise five acres one year and I can sell all my product and the next year I find I can sell the product of only one acre when I have raised five, obviously I am in a pretty precarious position. My father used to say to me when I was a boy, "Son, if I could be sure of selling my potatoes at fifty

Supply-A griculture

cents a hundred I would raise ten acres every year and I would feel quite secure." I do not suppose fifty cents would be sufficient now. That was back in the nineties and the early years of this century. The trouble was that some years you could not sell your potatoes; some years you could not even give them away.
We must establish stability of market. The question will be raised: How can you do that? There are two ways in which it can be done and our generation has pretty well indicated to us how it can be done. The first is this. We must see to it that the people are enabled to buy all of a given commodity that they can consume. Then what is surplus we must manage to put on the world market under a mutual aid scheme if needs be, under an UNRRA arrangement if necessary. Fluctuations in production from year to year could be taken care of through the world outlet. If we undertake to trade all our surplus we may be in difficulties. We can never be sure that we can trade off all that we can produce in a given year; but I do not think the time is likely to come, at least in our lives, when it will not be possible to distribute our surplus under mutual aid or under an UNRRA scheme.
The question will then arise: How will you pay for all that you distribute through mutual aid? Once more the problem is one of finance, and if you can produce enough in the dominion, and a sufficiently wide variety of commodities, it will be possible for you to keep your standard of living at whatever level your production will justify and also render available to the world your surplus. I am not going to go into great detail on that tonight. I may have more to say as the session progresses.

The question that arises is: how are we to sqlve this problem? I suggest in all sincerity that the only solution is going to be a wage bonus, a supplementary allowance to farm labourers over and above what the farmer can afford to pay. The orthodox economist will immediately find himself affected much as he would be if a galvanic needle were thrust into his spine. The important thing for him to bear in mind, however, is this: Can the dominion of Canada produce enough goods of a sufficient variety to enable her to pay the man who works on the farm milking cows and thinning beets and doing other things, $100 a month? The answer must be yes. If that is possible, then we must devise a financial system which will reflect the physical realities of our productive capacity and enable us to do financially what we can do physically.

I submit it is on the financial aspect of our economy that we must concentrate our attention. When we do that we shall find that it will be financially possible for us to distribute to the consumers of this country such an amount of purchasing power as will enable them to buy their full requirements of the goods we are able to produce, thereby guaranteeing our agriculturists a stable market so far as home consumption is concerned. A bushel of wheat will feed just as many men to-day as it did fifteen years ago or fifty years ago. It will feed quite as many men a year from to-day or ten years from to-day as it will feed to-day. Its price ought to be stable. It is for us to determine the means whereby to make it stable so that from year to year we shall know, and not only shall our producers know what they are going to get, but our governments are going to be able to calculate with some measure of accuracy what they may expect to derive by way of income from our producers. We shall be able to put our whole economy on a business basis, so that we shall have a chance to know where we stand. Everybody will grant that that is a wholly desirable objective. Let us determine by what mechanism we can attain that objective. We must have stable markets. We must know from year to year how much we can sell, and how much we can dispose of. To say that is impossible is, I think, a reckless remark; for certainly in any age which has heard the Atlantic charter advocate that all men should be guaranteed freedom from want, it should not sound absurd to propose that we should be able to render available to the people who need our goods and services, whatsoever in Canada we may have left over, after having provided for the needs of our own people.

Mr. Chairman, it is evident, after listening to the discussion in the committee yesterday and to-day that the farmers in this country are not very happy. We have heard many speeches, some of which were most entertaining, and all of which were interesting and instructive. They have been delivered by hon. members from all groups in the house, and representing widely separated sections of the country. The main theme in all of them seems to be that the condition of farming in this country is not satisfactory. All are agreed that unless it is satisfactory, the condition of other groups in the country will be jeopardized.
But when we begin to inquire into the causes of unrest in agriculture we become embroiled in a mass of facts and figures which, to say the least, are confusing, and which at one time seem to prove one thing and at another, something else. In the end they really do not prove very much of anything.
For this reason I hesitate to use figures at all, because I realize there is some truth in the old saying that figures lie and liars figure. However, I think I am quite safe in assuming that all hon. members in the committee, no matter how we may differ in our opinions about certain things, have enough confidence in the integrity and sincerity of each other to believe that no one of us will deliberately use figures with the intention of misleading. 
I have been trying to find a common base upon which to compare the income of farmers with that of other groups in the community. I was deeply interested in hearing the hon. member for Lethbridge use the year 1913, because recently a friend of mine gave me a graph of considerable interest. This graph, which I had not seen before, had been prepared by the Department of Pensions and National Health in 1937, and showed the index numbers of farm prices and industrial wages, taking the year 1913 as a base of 100.
Up to that time I had found that in some tables the period 1926-1929 was used. In still others I found the period 1935-1939. However, this was the first time I had seen the year 1913 used as a base. It seemed to me that whereas in that year industrial wages and farm prices were at exactly the same level, for that reason it was a fair year to take. I extended the graph from 1937 up to 1944, the last year for which I could get figures from the Department of Labour showing index numbers for wages.
I do not propose to draw any definite conclusions from the graph, because I am not an economist, and I do not know what the proper relationship is between the two lines which are shown. I frankly admit that as a farmer I look at this matter from a farmer's viewpoint. I dare say, however, that until I get other facts I cannot draw any definite conclusions. My only purpose in drawing this graph to the attention of the committee is to see if we can find out just what these figures imply.
For instance, we find that the index number of farm prices up to 1920 was above that of industrial wages. In comparison with the year 1913 when there was a base of 100, farm prices rose to 258-8 while industrial wages went only to 205-5, representing a difference of 53-3 points. In 1921 farm prices dropped 22-3 points below -wages, and they have been below ever since.
Surely there should be a more fair relationship between prices and wages than the figures I have mentioned would indicate. The period 1926-29 is usually considered the period in which we enjoyed most normal conditions, and in that year the difference was 28-7 points; that is, the index number of farm prices was 28-7 below that of industrial wages. During the thirties both farm prices and wages dropped disastrously, but in 1932 farm prices went to a low of 25 points below the 1913 figure, while wage rates were still 72-1 above the 1913 base. And in 1933 when wages were at their lowest point they were 63-3 points above the 1913 level.

In 1944, owing to subsidies, farm prices rose to 160-9, but wages rose to 263-9, or a difference of 103 points.

There is just one problem I wish to bring up at the present time. It arises out of a letter that I have received from the Bulkley valley, between Prince George and Prince Rupert. I will read the letter so that the Minister of Agriculture can give me a reply when he speaks later. The letter says in part:
The world is clamouring for wheat. Still the dominion government practically prohibits the Bulkley valley farmers from growing wheat and oats. The dominion government pays over $8 a ton for freight on pats shipped from the prairies to the Bulkley valley and Skeena river, plus more than $8 bonus per ton on wheat. As everybody knows, it is hard enough for Bulkley valley farmers to compete with the prairies growing wheat, but with the bonus against them it just stops them growing grain.
If it was to help the chicken farmers, why not bonus eggs instead? What excuse is there to pay the freight on oats to the lumber camps? Is the price of lumber too low?
I would ask the minister, is there not some way of bonusing the farmers in that section so that they may supply the needs of that area? They have the land available, and if they were given the bonus rather than the railways they could produce at a fair return to themselves.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext:
There is one point which I think the Minister of Agriculture has not covered in his remarks. I believe he was present at the food and agriculture organization meeting in Quebec City last October, where the need was expressed for the promotion of human welfare and for saving the world by providing it with the necessities of life. Noel Baker, the head of the British delegation, said at that conference that it was hunger that made Hitler. That conference did recognize the necessity for the food-
Supply-Agriculture

producing countries of the world tackling the problem of planning production in a worldwide way. Sir John Boyd Orr said:
If the nations of the world are going to get together to feed the peoples of the world, they must increase the production of our most important foods.
In many cases the production must be more than doubled.
In the face of that, the situation in Canada is alarming. During the past few years we have had hundreds of thousands of our men over in Europe, while food production was being carried on in this country in a noble way by those who remained on the farm. They did a great job. The fact that Canada can produce and did produce the food she did is one which no one can doubt. But -to-day there are more people here to do the work, and people better qualified to do the work. There is a tremendous demand for food production in Canada to-day. Yet we are faced with a butter shortage, shortages of other foods, and with rationing. At the same time we have 260,000 people unemployed in this country.
There is something seriously wrong when we have the power to produce, and when we have those unemployed seeking work and yet are not getting the needed production, because irrespective of what the minister said in regard to production in the years from 1942 to 1945 he will have to admit that in 1946 we are facing a serious reduction in food production all along the line as compared with the corresponding months of 1945. There must be a number of factors causing this reduction. What is needed at this time is a study of those factors which are causing a reduction in our food production at the very time when we and the whole world need food as never before. If we are to save this world we shall save it through food production to-day. If the united nations organization is to be successful it must be built on the basis of a world where the people who produce the food must receive a return that will pay them for their labour. If the nations who need our food cannot pay for the produce we are selling, let the facts be presented to us and then we can decide upon the next step.
As has been said by a previous speaker, there is evidence in everything which emanates from farm organizations, whether in expressions of opinion or formal resolutions, that those engaged in agricultural production are not satisfied. There are factors which are definitely working against the production of food, and it is our duty to study what those factors are and decide upon a solution. I will submit to the minister one or two points

which have arisen in my own experience. We find in the reports tabled by various organizations, in the statistical records, in general information received and from conversations with those actually engaged in the production of food, what are the considerations uppermost in the minds of those who are going out of production.
In proof of what I have said, the figures in the monthly dairy review of Canada issued by the bureau of statistics show, as I believe I stated about a month ago, that the following reductions have occurred in percentages of creamery butter produced in Canada since the beginning of the present year, as compared with the corresponding period of 1945: January, 15-6; February, 18-3; March, 19-6; April, 8-8. The production of cheddar cheese in Canada was 27-8 per cent less than in the same month of 1945; in February the reduction was 36-5 per cent; in March, 35-5 per cent; in April 33 per cent. The figures with regard to the production of hogs have ahead}' been admitted by the minister. I think his explanation is that the production of hogs and cattle, particularly in the winter time, depends upon the amount of feed that is grown; and since the volume of coarse grains grown in Canada was much smaller, there was bound to be some reduction. But the farmers who previously raised -hogs have shown that, even though they had had the feed, they had no inclination to resume this line of production, that they would not bother feeding grain to hogs. That is true in the west, and there must be some reason.
Farm organizations, and particularly the United Farmers of Canada, have urged a more realistic plan to stimulate food production in Canada, Among their recommendations was one relative to farm Jabour. Surely these problems are not insurmountable. If Canada could produce these products in war time she can produce them in peace time. If people who are out of work are reluctant to undertake farm labour there must be something hindering them. Is it the fact that there is no adequate return for their work? What is the solution?
In his speech to-day the minister made a curious explanation as to what in his opinion is wrong with agriculture. He said we all know that people like to grow things, that they desire to produce food and clothing for mankind. If that attitude is an indication of his policy I believe his policy has been wrong. You kill the desire of people to grow things, whether for food or for clothing, if you require them to grow these supplies without giving them the necessary return.

speechtext: Hear, hear. The profit motive.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: After these long years of drought and anxiety the farmer needs a return for his labour. If you are going to provide it-

speechtext: Private enterprise.

Private enterprise?
Like the grain exchange? Money was made by those who operate on the grain exchange, and the people who consume the products pay more too, but not to the farmer. That is where your trouble is. Nobody will go on a farm and work year after year under those conditions. True, the farmer likes to see things growing; he wants to help in production, but from long experience he has learned that at the end of it all there is no guarantee that he will have something for his labour. Year after year the lack of return on the investment he has in his farm, and the weight of the mortgage he cannot pay back, mean a constant piling up of debt which cannot be met. Finally it means that he must leave the farm, because the mortgage company forecloses, and then it sells the place to somebody else when another crop of farmers comes along. That is your "private enterprise" for you. The chaps who run these mortgage and loan companies lend the farmer money when prices are high and collect when wheat goes down to thirty or forty cents a bushel.
