The farmers of Canada stated in their brief that there must be an immediate cancellation of the federal tax of three cents per gallon on gasoline used for agricultural purposes. They also insisted that there must be an immediate revision of the Income War Tax Act to eliminate inequalities in the application of the act to farming operations. After talking to farmers during the past, year, I do not believe there is one single thing about which complaints have been more general. Cases are cited where a farmer, not being permitted by the laws of this country to deliver his grain in 1942 and 1943. delivered it in 1944, and then the income tax officials came around and collected on the basis of his income from cash sales in 1944 in respect of grain raised and income earned in 1942-and 1943. I suggest, perhaps not to the Minister of Agriculture direct but through him to the Minister of National Revenue, that the time is long past when the government should go into the whole matter of farm income tax and put it on an equitable basis.
The present system is entirely unjust in the light of conditions which have prevailed over so many years. Half the year in the prairie country there is no production. The minister admits that if for four or five years you have crops, you may then expect to go for four or five years with no production.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: Not "no" production; low production.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: Yes. He also stated the facts when he said that production is so low that it does not cover the cost of operation during those drought years of which he spoke, when the farmer was going into debt year after year. In 1941, 1942, 1943, and to a greater extent in 1944 and 1945 the farmer found he had some income over and above his cost of production. What did he do with it? He turned over the money to pay off his debts; and the figures which have been placed before the house show the admirable way in which he did so. Now he finds, having discharged the debts he incurred in the thirties and early forties, a heavy income tax is placed on him for the years 1942, 1943 and 1944.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: Then he has to go to the mortgage company to borrow money to pay his income tax.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext:
Many cases have been reported to me where farmers have had to go to the bank and borrow the money to meet their heavy income tax. I suggest to the minister that revisions of the act in one or two respects would do a great deal to increase agricultural production on the prairies. Number one would be to allow as an exemption on his income tax any debts paid by a farmer which were incurred prior to 1940, in years when he had low production. Secondly, allowance should be made in that income tax form for wages to the farmer's wife and those of his children sixteen years of age and over who are working on the farm. To put the combined earnings of these people, as they are on the farm, on one man and charge him on anything in excess of $1,200 is patently unfair. Similar groups of people living anywhere else and putting in the long hours that are put in by the farmer and his family-the farmer working fifteen hours a day and his wife and children anywhere from ten or twelve to fifteen hours-would not be treated in that way. There must be some justice in this scheme of things if we are ever to get people back on a producing basis. The farmers feel this injustice deeply, and their natural reaction, for which you cannot blame them, is this: "Is it to be said that
Supply-Agriculture

after working these extra hours raising hogs, feeding chickens, raising turkeys, getting up early and milking cows and working the cream separator, no allowance is to be made us? There is only one thing we can do, because it is not worth it; we will simply produce to the $1,500 level and live as best we can, cutting down our hours of labour to ten or twelve instead of fifteen, and in some cases, eighteen."
The farm organizations of Canada have also stated that some action should be taken to halt the practice of sales of flour with mill feeds sold to farmers. In eastern Canada there has been a common practice among people selling feeds to farmers to stipulate that if they want so many sacks of feed they must take so many sacks of flour along with it. Perhaps it was not put exactly in that way, but the farmer did actually have to take flour in order to get feed.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: It is against the regulations to do that now.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: I believe it is against the regulations now.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: And has been for some time.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: When was it stopped?

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: An attempt was made to stop it two or three years ago. I am not saying that it has been stopped, but it is against the regulations. You cannot, however, prevent a farmer from taking home flour if he goes to buy feed and he sees flour in the store selling at a certain price. If he wishes to take it home and mix it with the feed which he has. at home there is no way of stopping him.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: That is not the case to which I refer.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: It is the kind of case.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: I am speaking of actual cases where the farmer has been told that if he wanted to take home feed he must take so many sacks of flour.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext:
That was the position taken by the mills for a long period of years, that if you wished to get feed you had to take a certain proportion of flour. I understand it was first instituted by the mills, and the dealers were told that if they wanted half a carload of feed they must fill the car up with flour. At first it was a practice. on the part of the mills themselves and later on, during the war, we had a provision requiring that cars should not be shipped partly filled. That, however, had nothing to do with feed or flour. It was due to the shortage of rolling 
stock to carry all the freight that had to be moved during war time. Some of the boards stated that cars had to be loaded to full capacity. When we attempted to enforce the regulation with regard to farmers taking feed we were confronted with that fact. We were told that if a man wanted only three-quarters of a car of feed they could not sell it unless they could fill the car, and he would take flour to fill it. Of course it was stated that this was carried out to the dealer, who said to the farmer, "If you want to get the amount of feed that you have ordered you must take so much flour"; and the farmer in some cases, I presume, took lower grades of flour home and mixed it with the feed he had and fed it. Attempts have been made to stop that kind of thing, but there are cases where the farmers find it to their advantage to feed flour. They have taken a lower grade of flour, particularly since wheat has gone up and flour has been maintained on the basis of 78 cents. The farmer walks into a shop and sees a bag of flour there, and he decides that it is to his advantage to buy the flour rather than buy wheat at $1.55 or $1.25 a bushel. So he buys the flour and mixes it himself along with the feed he has and he feeds it. I do not know any way of stopping that by law. It is a practice that has obtained.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: I understand that side of it, but there were cases where farmers were practically compelled to take home flour a couple of years ago.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: That was true some time ago.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: The farmers' organizations wanted it stopped because in many cases the flour was more than they could use themselves. It was a result of the milling industry being overstocked with flour; there was a heavy demand for feed and they did not have shipping space to send it overseas.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext: There was a heavy demand for mill feeds such as bran and shorts, in the United States and elsewhere, which could have been sold to better advantage there, and consequently pressure was put on.

maintopic: ESTIMATES 1946-47
speechtext:
The fact remains that the world requires that flour to feed people and I hope the practice will be completely stopped. I presume it will be stopped, because there will not be the same shortage, and flour will be in too great a demand throughout the world.
The other department that links itself with food production is not under the minister, but a statement was given this afternoon with regard to the number of veterans. I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture, with the

Supply-Agriculture
assistance of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, give consideration to the fact that there are
18,000	returned men who have qualified as farmers. Everything possible should be done at an early date; some emergency measures should be taken, to see that these men get on their land and get into production for the crop of 1946. In another month it will be too late. I have letters. from my constituency indicating that men have qualified and have been allocated land, but some inspections have not been completed or for some other reason they are being held up. Surely where these men have qualified under the regulations under the Veterans Land Act, where they have proved themselves to be farmers and men of sound judgment, they should be left to choose the land. It should be left to them if they are considered fit to be farmers, having some idea of what an economic piece of land is.
I understand the minister's difficulty and I appreciate his anxiety to avoid some of the errors that occurred under the old soldier settlement board. But here are 18,000 young men, many of them married, who want to get started, and the world is in need of production. I urge the ministers to get together and do all *hey can to wipe out the red tape that is preventing these young men from getting into production, because they should be seeding to-day. Seeding in the west is pretty well on and in some parts practically completed.
A good deal has been said-the subject has been referred to in every speech that has been made-with regard to increases in farm prices. This party has supported the government in its efforts by means of price ceilings to prevent inflation; we are going to stay with the government in the maintenance of prices, and we demand that these prices be not broken. There must be a proper relation between cost of production and the value of the farmers' products. If the government will stand firmly by this principle they will bring security into the minds and hearts of the farmers, and that is something that is valuable. But we will oppose them every time they puncture these ceilings. That position should be made clear. That is why we opposed the agricultural implement increase without a corresponding increase in farm prices. If the farm prices are raised there is an increase in the cost of living and a spiral will be started, as the minister has already said. A proper relation between cost of production and farm prices would give security to the farmer, the thing that is most important to him, the thing that would keep him on the farm, the thing that will attract others to the farm. There are many more people who would enjoy producing and who would like to be producing than are on the
farms to-day, but they will not dare go on the farms because of the lack of security. If security can be guaranteed they will go at it. The same thing applies to the wages that are paid, and also to the cost of living. If there is a proper relationship existing there, there will not be much trouble with labour. If an increase is to be allowed on only one line without a corresponding increase in the other, then trouble can be expected from labour.
We do not believe, as do our hon. friends to the right, that the ceiling should be lifted. We went through a depression following a spiral of prices in the inflationary period and we do not want to go through that again.

Another thing I should like to advocate to the minister is the establishment of the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency of Canada's grain. The thing which farmers dislike to see is the bringing in of an agency such as the grain exchange at the time when farmers are out producing at a minimum re-
Supply-Agriculture

turn themselves, when everybody is doing his utmost to produce at a time when the world is in such a difficult situation. To see an organization like the Winnipeg grain exchange reinstated in the marketing field and start gambling in food would be a bitter blow to the people and would work to the detriment of food production throughout the world. If the farmers are guaranteed that security the minister need have no fear of what Canadian people will do with regard to farm production. Guarantee them a proper relationship over a period of years and you will get the best returns from the farmers. You will get more economic production and you will have the farmer in a position where he can produce economically because he can afford to buy the machinery to produce efficiently. You will have prosperity among the farmers which will give prosperity to the state. You will have a prosperous industry which will not only make the greatest contribution to the welfare of the people of Canada but provide the people of the world the food which is most essential to the maintenance of peace and to the future well-begin of our people. It is the only hope of humanity if it ever expects or hopes to live in a world where there are no wars.
